Boston Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy knows his team has figured out the Tampa Bay Rays pretty well this season.
That said, the Red Sox (84-70) still can learn more about the Rays (93-60) when the teams meet Saturday afternoon in St. Petersburg, Fla.
"At this point with (the Rays), we've played them enough already," Tracy said. "We have a pretty good understanding of them, (and) they have a pretty good understanding of us. But you could always pick up more stuff."
In Friday's series opener, the Red Sox scored four runs over the first three innings and won 4-2 to snap Tampa Bay's six-game winning streak and improve to 6-5 this season vs. the Rays.
Boston currently holds the second wild-card position in the American League but is dealing with several injuries.
"We have guys beat up that aren't here, and the hope is we get people healthy, and the roster could look even different a week from now than it does right now," Tracy said.
Boston's Willson Contreras is day-to-day after getting hit on the hand, while closer Aroldis Chapman (lat tightness) has been unavailable the past two contests.
Right-hander Tanner Houck (Tommy John surgery in 2025) and lefty Garrett Crochet (left shoulder inflammation) have advanced in their rehab assignments.
Boston left-hander Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.02 ERA) is expected to make his 26th start on Saturday and will try to record his sixth consecutive win.
Tolle is 1-0 with an 0.75 ERA over 12 innings in his last two starts, allowing one run on eight hits while striking out 19 with a walk. He is 0-2 with a 4.50 ERA in two starts and one relief outing against Tampa Bay, which already has clinched a playoff berth.
Whatever Rays pitching coach Kyle Snyder and the rest of the staff have done with trade-deadline acquisition Freddy Peralta certainly has been a success.
Acquired by the club from the New York Mets for three prospects on Aug. 2, Peralta (9-11, 4.67 ERA) -- a right-hander who will start for the Rays on Saturday -- arrived from the Big Apple as a lesser version of what he was during his two All-Star seasons with the Milwaukee Brewers.
He was 5-9 with a 4.99 ERA with the Mets, but the work was immediately put in by the Rays to adjust Peralta to where he was when he was a 17-game winner with a sub-3.00 ERA last season.
"For some reason, when I got here, when I sat here with Kyle and (bullpen coach Jorge Moncada) and (manager Kevin Cash), they told me, like, 'You're gonna do what you want to do here, and we are going to help you to do it,'" Peralta said.
"And we know what you need to do to make those adjustments. We just put everything on the table. I just followed all the instructions, and it's what I am right now."
With the Rays, Peralta is 4-2 with a 3.86 ERA in eight starts, but his past four outings have been gems. He has pitched 23 innings and has allowed just two runs on 10 hits, with 17 strikeouts, four walks and an 0.78 ERA in that span.
"Fastball Freddy," who is using his changeup much more with the Rays, is 0-2 with a 5.40 ERA in three career starts against Boston.
Peralta allowed two runs on three hits in 4 1/3 innings in a 4-0 loss at Boston on July 11 while with the Mets.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — A year ago, as the Red Sox crept toward the end of the regular season, the pitching choices for their looming Wild Card Series in New York were limited. Beyond ace Garrett Crochet, who dominated the Yankees in Game 1, the Red Sox ended up going with the unreliable Brayan Bello in Game 2 and the untested Connelly Early in Game 3. Two losses later, they were packing their bags for the winter.
This year, with a replay of that series feeling all but certain to begin a week from Tuesday and once again in the Bronx, the pitching plans look nothing like they did back then.
Which is good news for the Red Sox.
Even with Crochet sidelined all season by injury, the pitching rotation has been, in the words of interim manager Chad Tracy, “pivotal” to the drastic midseason turnaround that lifted this team from the depths of the American League standings and into the playoff race.
A trade for Sonny Gray. The continued development of Payton Tolle. And the free agent signing of Ranger Suarez. Three big moves, three likely starters for one more entry in the ongoing Boston/New York postseason clash of baseball titans.
Friday night in Florida, it was Suarez’s turn to prove his readiness. Facing the first-place Rays presented an obvious test, but for Suarez, it also was a chance to build on his two previous starts, in which he allowed only one run in 14 innings. As Tracy pointed out before the game, there is no mystery into what makes a good Suarez outing. Control the tempo, get ahead in the count, and locate pitches. When the lefthander does those three things, he can be pretty hard to beat.
But, as the Rays learned Friday, even if he doesn’t quite do those three things as well as he wants to, he can still find a way to battle through.
So there he was at the end of a decidedly mixed bag of a night, leading the Sox to a 4-2 win, improving his record to 8-4 after giving up just one run in 5⅔ innings. On the upside, he struck out five and consistently got key outs in key moments.
On the downside, he had to labor mightily to get there, walking a career-high five batters, throwing just 56 of his 98 pitches for strikes. He got away with it this time, but come the playoffs, that’s playing with fire, whether against the Yankees or perhaps the Rays again, with Tampa Bay in line to host the wild-card winners.
The Sox chose to take the positive out of the night.
“When I issued those walks, I think that the game was taking me to a place that wasn’t the right one. So I just tried to take a deep breath and slow it down, and I was able to then take it from there,” Suarez said.
He struck out Yandy Díaz to end the second inning, stranding two runners on base. He got out of another jam in the third, a Chandler Simpson hard-hit line out to right and a strikeout of Jonny DeLuca to strand two more runners.
Suarez did it again in the fourth, helping his own cause by starting a nifty inning-ending double play, snaring Taylor Walls’s line drive to the mound and then throwing to first to double off Nick Fortes.
A clean fifth ended on a called third strike to Junior Caminero, but gave way to a messier sixth, with a leadoff walk to Ryan Vilade eventually leading Tracy to pull the plug as Suarez approached 100 pitches. But not before he struck out DeLuca to get the first out.
“He’s a very good competitor and a really good pitcher,” Tracy said, “that even when he’s got traffic, you trust that he’s going to find his way through it. . . . He walked five, but still almost completed six innings. He was very competitive with men on base.”
“I got traffic every single inning because of the walks, but I was able to limit damage today, and that was part of it,” Suarez said. “It was one of those nights that you didn’t have the command, but I was able to turn the page quickly and was able to get outs when I needed.”
Good as the escape act was, it’s all just staging for what comes next, a playoff berth the Red Sox could clinch on Saturday. Suarez was signed in part because of his experience in the postseason, earned across eight seasons with the Phillies. Suarez is 4-1 with a 1.48 ERA in 11 playoff appearances, which includes eight starts. He was the winner of Game 3 of the 2022 World Series, beating the eventual champion Astros with five shutout innings.
The Phillies also called on him to come out of the bullpen in Game 5 of the NLCS, and all he did was earn his first postseason save by getting two outs on two pitches, stranding the winning run and clinching the Series berth.
“When you get to this part of the season, not every outing is going to go perfectly. But he’s been there and done that as far as navigating his way through an outing and finding a way to strand base runners,” Tracy said. “The game’s not going to speed up on him. You know, even if he’s walked some and there’s some people on base, he doesn’t ever look like he speeds up. He just keeps making his pitches.”

ST. PETERSBURG – As they head into the final 10 days of the regular season, the Red Sox are monitoring a plethora of injuries to key players.
Given that the Sox still hold firm possession of the second American League Wild Card spot and could clinch a berth as early as this weekend, the plan will be to operate conservatively in hopes of getting everyone healthy for the games that count the most.
Here is an update on where things stand with those key players.
First baseman Willson Contreras
There was a big scare on Thursday night in Texas when the team’s most productive hitter this season was pelted on the top of his right hand with a pitch in the top of the eighth and immediately exited the game. Contreras said that in the moment, it felt like a fracture. Fortunately, X-rays taken at the ballpark were negative.
While interim manager Chad Tracy mentioned the possibility of follow-up imaging, there was none on Friday. Contreras didn’t have his hand taped and spent his share of time in the training room.
Where do things stand?
“Obviously, sore with some swelling,” Tracy said. “So nothing new other than just over the next couple of days, they'll work on treatment, on getting the swelling out, see if he can get grip strength back, and then we'll go from there. So just day to day.”
Could there still be additional scans?
“Not right now. Right now, with the initial one, they're optimistic,” said Tracy. “Just work on the swelling and see how he progresses over the next couple days, and then determine if they feel like they need more. But right now, they're just going to work on that.”
Closer Aroldis Chapman
When Garrett Whitlock closed Thursday’s win in Texas, it was obvious something was up with Chapman. It turns out he has been dealing with lat tightness he sustained while working out prior to Tuesday’s game.
Chapman downplayed the injury on Friday, saying the team is being conservative and that he felt healthy enough to play catch before the opener of the three-game series against the Rays. The Red Sox told him not to.
The lefty fireballer said he won’t pitch this weekend, but he expects to return during the final homestand, which starts on Tuesday.
“I’m not worried at all,” Chapman said. “From the first time I felt it to today, I feel very good. I was going to go out and throw, but the team wants to take it slow, and they want me to take my time.“
It is all about being 100% for the first game of the playoffs on Sept. 29, right?
“Yeah, of course,” said Chapman. “A hundred percent.”
Center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela
Boston’s All-Star center fielder hasn’t played since Sept. 2 due to a right quad strain. It sounds unlikely he’ll be able to play in a rehab game for Triple-A Worcester because that season ends on Sunday. But Tracy is confident with where Rafaela is at.
“I think he got close to 90% of his acceleration yesterday,” said Tracy. “So not ready yet, but he's moving quickly in the right direction, which is good. If he doesn’t play [for Worcester], there is a goal of getting him some live at-bats of some kind. You know, like live BP-type at-bats of some kind, plus the Trajekt. The important thing is that the running piece keeps going in the right direction.”
Left-hander Garrett Crochet
Boston’s ace, who has been out since April 25 due to a left shoulder injury, is still racing against the clock to try to pitch in relief during the postseason. His next step will be on Saturday, when he throws his second up-and-down bullpen session of the week at Fenway Park.
For Crochet to have any shot at pitching at the start of the postseason, he would have to start facing hitters by next week.
“I would say we're to the point where these next five days or so are going to be pretty telling,” said Tracy. “How does the side go, and what can we do with him early next week? And that'll give us a better idea of the answer to that question.”
Right-hander Tanner Houck
The righty will make the fourth and final appearance of his Minor League rehab assignment when he throws roughly 50 pitches for Worcester on Saturday. It’s possible Houck will get a tuneup or two in regular-season action for the Red Sox next week, which could give the club a better gauge if he’s a possibility to pitch in the playoffs. Houck had Tommy John surgery 13 months ago.

RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses the latest on a number of key injured Red Sox players. Be sure to join our FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
Ahead of the Boston Red Sox series opener at Tropicana Field against the Tampa Bay Rays on Friday, interim manager Chad Tracy met with the media and provided updates on a number of injured Red Sox players.
Here's what you need to know:
All eyes were on the All-Star first baseman after Thursday night's win over the Texas Rangers. Contreras exited the game in the eighth inning after being hit by a pitch on the right-hand. According to MassLive.com's Chris Cotillo, Contreras told reporters after the game that the injury "felt" like a fracture. While initial X-Rays were negative, as the team learned with infielder Curtis Mead, that doesn't mean Contreras was completely out of the woods yet. According to MLB.com's Ian Browne, the team is waiting for swelling in the 34-year-old's hand to subside before testing his grip strength to determine if additional testing is needed.
Contreras is out of the lineup for Friday's series opener.
Crochet threw a 30-pitch up-and-down bullpen session on Tuesday back at Fenway Park, representing the most labor-intensive of the four throwing sessions the 27-year-old has done since restarting a throwing progression Aug. 3. According to WEEI's Rob Bradford, Crochet will throw another side session on Saturday as he continues to work his way back from left shoulder inflammation that has kept him out since April 29.
After turning to Garrett Whitlock to lock down Thursday's win, Tracy told reporters, including Cotillo, that Chapman was unavailable with LAT tightness. According to Bradford, Chapman said the injury popped up ahead of Tuesday's series opener in Texas and that he wasn't concerned about the injury, saying the latest he would return to the mound would be during the team's upcoming home stand, beginning on Tuesday night, if he doesn't make an appearance in Tampa.
Tyron Guerrero
After landing on the injured list on Sept. 1 with right shoulder inflammation. The 35-year-old flamethrower was expected to be activated when he was first eligible, ahead of Wednesday's game in Texas. However, after experiencing lower back tightness, the team delayed his activation. According to Bradford, Guerrero "felt fine" after throwing 20 pitches off the mound on Friday afternoon. However, it still remains unclear when he may be activated.
The 32-year-old outfielder landed on the injured list last Friday with a "right foot ligament injury" after getting it caught in the grates along the center field wall in the Sept. 8 loss to the Los Angeles Angels. As Bradford noted, White has been diagnosed with a ligament tear, likely ending his season.
White's injury seems to open the door for Spring Training standout Braiden Ward to join the Red Sox as a fourth outfielder/pinch runner in the playoffs.
Up next for the Sox
The Red Sox will look to carry the momentum from Thursday's come-from-behind win into the final road series of the year against the Rays. Ranger Suarez (7-4, 3.33 ERA) will get the start for the Red Sox opposite Ian Seymour (9-6, 4.27 ERA) for the Rays. First pitch from Tropicana Field is set for 7:10 p.m. ET.

Boston Red Sox fans were already going through it on Thursday night after Willson Contreras left the series finale against the Texas Rangers early after being hit by a pitch on the hand. Seeing Garrett Whitlock emerge from the bullpen to close a 4-3 game in the ninth inning only made fears worse.
Whitlock is no slouch, as Red Sox fans know, and he got through the ninth frame unscathed, but fans expect to see Aroldis Chapman in moments like that. After the game, Boston announced that Chapman was unavailable due to a lat issue.
Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said in his September 17 postgame presser that Chapman has been dealing with lat tightness for a couple of days but that he's been improving lately. Boston has classified him as day-to-day and it will routinely check on his recovery progress to gauge his availability.
The best news from Tracy on Chapman is that the team will not place him on the injured list. The Sox's bullpen has been one of their deadliest weapons all season and Chapman with his 1.95 ERA, 34 saves, blistering velocity and unmatched consistency at 38 years old has been a huge part of that success.
Aroldis Chapman injury news is a blow the Red Sox's bullpen can't afford as the playoffs near
Still, having Chapman at anything less than 100 percent is dangerous this late in the season with the playoffs on the horizon. In a tight game, one slip-up in the ninth inning could lead to disaster.
The rest of the Red Sox's bullpen is hardly in its best shape. Justin Slaten's season ended following continued flexor issues and Tyron Guerrero is still on the IL bouncing back from shoulder inflammation. Erik Miller is also dealing with a mechanical issue that has severely impacted his command over his last two outings.
If Chapman's injury is as mild as Tracy is letting on and he doesn't need an IL stint, Boston might be able to avoid disaster. But it also needs Chapman's help to clinch its playoff spot in the first place. The offense is struggling to get out to enough of a lead that it doesn't need Chapman to hold a slim margin in the late innings, but that won't fly in the postseason, especially with an injured closer.
At least the Red Sox expect some relief reinforcements in the coming days. Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet are working towards returns from long-term injuries in a relief role and they could take some pressure off the 'pen, but neither could fill Chapman's role.

Alec Gamboa, who played for the Lotte Giants in the KBO League last year. He failed to re-sign with Lotte, but a year later he debuted in the major leagues and is aiming to make the postseason roster.
On the 18th (Korean time) at Globe Life Field in Arlington, Texas, in the game against the Texas Rangers, Gamboa came in with one out in the eighth inning and no runners on, recorded 2/3 of an inning, allowed one hit and no runs, and earned a hold. It was his second hold of the season.
That day Gamboa entered the game after Trevor Story hit a go-ahead three-run homer in the top of the eighth to put them up 4-3. Starter Sonny Gray pitched well with 6 1/3 innings, three hits (one home run), three walks, six strikeouts and three runs, and second pitcher Wyatt Alls recorded one inning, one strikeout and no runs.
Gamboa came in to face a left-handed batting lineup of Corey Seager and Josh Young. He gave up a single to the first batter, Seager, to right field. Later, he fell behind Josh Young 3-1 in the count but induced a shortstop grounder with a low 95.6-mph sinker, producing a double play to end the inning.
After recording his first hold in his debut by getting Lee Jung-hoo and others out in the Aug. 22 game against the San Francisco Giants, he recorded his second hold of the season. Gamboa's season performance is excellent. In 19 appearances he pitched 29 2/3 innings with 1 win, 2 holds, 1 save, a 1.21 ERA, a .216 batting average against and a 1.04 WHIP.
That day closer Aroldis Chapman could not take the mound because of trapezius muscle stiffness, and another lefty in the high-leverage group, Eric Miller, had earlier shown instability on the 17th against Texas by allowing three runs on 22 pitches in one inning. As a result, rookie right-hander Wyatt Alls and left-hander Gamboa had to take on the high-leverage roles, and setup man Garrett Whitlock had to assume the closer role. All of them then held the one-run lead.
Acting manager Chad Tracy praised Alls and Gamboa's high-leverage performances, saying, "They were really great. They were inserted suddenly into important situations. At times they had to take the mound with the lead, and they did really well."
Gamboa once again successfully passed a high-leverage test for the high-leverage group. Now the question is whether he can join Boston's postseason journey. Boston has a 83-70 record and sits second in the wild-card standings. They are five games ahead of the third-place Cleveland Guardians, so barring an upset they are all but certain to secure the 5 seed.
Over the Monster, which reports on Boston news, listed Gamboa in the "pitchers who need to prove themselves" spot while predicting the postseason roster. The outlet said, "He is a player who had a pleasantly surprising performance this year. He even made two starts as an opener. In recent weeks the bullpen has had injuries, and combined with his own performance, he has risen to the point of being used in higher-stakes, high-leverage situations."
Closers Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Eric Miller, Tyrone Guerrero and Garrett Crochet are confirmed. It is likely that one more left-handed reliever will be added and the rest filled with right-handers.
They went on to say, "If Aroldis Chapman, Eric Miller and Garrett Crochet are the confirmed left-handed bullpen pieces, the final left-handed spot could be a competition between Hobani Moran and Gamboa," and added, "If I had to pick the final four now, I would choose Brayan Bello, Tanner Houck, Moran and Gamboa," predicting they would make the postseason roster.
Boston regional outlet MassLive also highlighted the performances of Gamboa and Alls on the 17th, saying, "He seized an unexpected opportunity this year, expanded his standing, and his entry into the postseason roster race—which would have been hard to imagine just a few weeks ago—is worthy of high praise," introducing that Gamboa has performed well enough to be included on the postseason roster.
Gamboa was drafted by the Los Angeles Dodgers in the ninth round, 281st overall, in the 2019 draft. But he couldn't break through the Dodgers' deep minor league system, and last year he joined the KBO League's Lotte Giants as a replacement player and delivered a sensational performance.
He had an especially strong performance, including being named player of the month for June, but fatigue accumulated late in the season and elbow pain caused him to miss several turns in the rotation, preventing a smooth finish. His KBO League stats were 19 games, 108 innings, 7 wins, 8 losses and a 3.58 ERA.
Although Gamboa failed to re-sign with Lotte, he said of going to Lotte, "It was a good opportunity to show myself elsewhere. I wanted to experience a bigger and new environment than Triple-A in the U.S. I believed I would show good pitching there, return to the U.S. and seize another opportunity," and added, "Before going to Korea I had never been abroad. Experiencing another country, seeing how polite the people there are and how much they love baseball, and seeing what style of baseball they play was really fun," saying it was an opportunity that lifted his spirits.
Was failing to re-sign with Lotte a blessing in disguise? After signing a minor league deal with Boston he made an emotional big league debut and now stands on the verge of making the postseason roster. Gamboa is becoming a symbol of a life turnaround.

RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses starter Sonny Gray joining Red Sox Hall of Famer Tim Wakefield in franchise history. Be sure to join our FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
The Boston Red Sox avoided a sweep at the hands of the Texas Rangers on Thursday night thanks to a 4-3 win that was powered by an eighth-inning, go-ahead, three-run home run off the bat of shortstop Trevor Story. While Story's big swing was undoubtedly the story of the game, Boston was in position to win because of Sonny Gray's fantastic start, a start that saw him join Red Sox Hall of Famer Tim Wakefield in the history books.
Gray tossed 6.1 innings, allowing just three earned runs on three hits while striking out six and walking three. According to Red Sox Nation Stats on Twitter/X, Gray became the first pitcher aged 36 or older to log 21 or more starts of six or more innings pitched since Wakefield did so in 2008.
Gray has been nothing short of a revelation since arriving in Boston on an offseason deal with the St. Louis Cardinals. The 36-year-old veteran was brought in, in part, to be the "Robin" to Garrett Crochet's "Batman." However, because of the shoulder injury that has kept Crochet out of the rotation since late April, Gray has served as "Batman" just as well as the 2025 American League Cy Young Award runner-up could have.
In Crochet's absence, Gray has posted a 2.57 ERA in 23 starts, spanning 140 innings pitched. The team has gone 17-6 in those starts. Not only has Gray been Boston's best starter since the Crochet injury, but he's also been one of the best arms in baseball in the stretch, with his ERA ranking as the sixth-lowest mark over that time.
Overall, Gray has posted a 2.82 ERA that ranks fifth best among all American League starters, doing it in 163 innings with an fWAR of 3.2 that sits just outside the top 10 at No. 11. Perhaps most importantly, even when the 36-year-old veteran doesn't have his best stuff, he keeps the team in a position to win, as was evident on Thursday night.
When Gray was first acquired, many questioned whether he could still be a top of the rotation arm. Now, after answering those questions with a season that'll likely see him finish top five in American League Cy Young Award voting, the only question that remains is whether he'll return for 2027 and beyond.
Up next for the Sox
After dropping two of three in Texas, the Red Sox' final regular-season road trip rolls on as they open a three-game series at Tropicana Field against the likely American League East champion Tampa Bay Rays on Friday night. Ranger Suarez (7-4, 3.33 ERA) gets the start for Boston opposite Ian Seymour (9-6, 4.27 ERA) for Tampa Bay. First pitch is set for 7:10 p.m. ET.

The Boston Red Sox acquired Johan Oviedo from the Pittsburgh Pirates in the winter, thinking he would be their No. 5 starter.
However, Connelly Early won that job in spring training, and Oviedo was relegated to the bullpen. Near the end of spring training, his velocity was noticeably down, and he gave up six hits and four earned runs in his only outing for the Red Sox this year. He was placed on the injured list with an elbow sprain and pitched in a rehab game with Triple-A Worcester on Thursday.
His velocity was back up, topping out at 98.5 mph and averaging 95.9 mph with his fastball. That is where the Red Sox expected him to be when they got him. The Red Sox could use a starter right now, but just like Garrett Crochet, there is not time to get Oviedo built up as a starter.
"You always have great dreams about playing for a team like (Boston) with a lot of history," Oviedo said, per MassLive's Katie Morrison-O'Day. "You want to fill up your spot, and not being available to help the team from the beginning definitely has been a challenge for me. If I still have a shot to help the team in any way, in the last few weeks of the season or the playoffs, I'm just trying to be ready."
"I'm more than open to fill any role, and not finish the season on the IL," Oviedo added. "It's definitely not the plan for any pitcher. But all I'm trying to do right now is be healthy and be available for the team if they need me.
Oviedo pitched 2 1/3 innings on Thursday, notching four strikeouts. He gave up one run, two hits and a walk, landing 20 of his 30 pitches for strikes. He threw his four-seamer, slider, sinker, curveball and changeup in the outing.
Oviedo is a talented pitcher, and it's very possible that he would have been a staple in the rotation this year had he not gotten hurt. The minor league season is about to end, so there won't be many more opportunities for him to get rehab outings. He is unsure if he will be on the taxi squad or get to pitch for the Red Sox this year. However, he wants to be ready if his number is called.
"I've been on a playoff roster before but never pitched," Oviedo said. "So it's definitely one of the dreams that I want to accomplish. If Boston will give me that chance, if the team needs me, hopefully I can be ready for it."

Boston's rotation is in solid shape even with Garrett Crochet (left shoulder inflammation) missing most of the year, but Oviedo -- if he can return in time -- could make an impact as a multi-inning reliever down the stretch or in the postseason.

item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas — Nearly three months after Caleb Durbin first dislocated his left pinkie and more than a month after he reinjured it, the third baseman’s digit remains locked nearly at a right angle.
“It doesn’t quite straighten or bend all the way,” Durbin acknowledged.
Durbin received X-rays after his initial injury against the Rockies on June 24 and the reinjury against the White Sox on Aug. 6. In both instances, there was no fracture and he was told playing was simply a matter of pain tolerance.
And so, there was little question about how he’d proceed. He didn’t seek more information.
“There really is kind of a joint understanding [with the team] that we’ll get it looked at at the end of the season if we have to, because [whatever the diagnosis is], it’s not going to impact my decision to play at all,” he said.
Still, Durbin recognizes fingers shouldn’t look like they could be used to mount a shelf. Might he require offseason surgery?
“I don’t know yet. We’ll find out,” he said. “I hope there’s something we can do about it. But we’ll get there when the time comes.”
For now, Durbin remains a lineup constant. Thursday’s contest against the Rangers marked his 145th game of the season. He continues to deliver Gold Glove-caliber defense (his six outs above average lead AL third basemen) while also pushing the envelope on the field with high-IQ plays, most recently advancing from first to third on an infield single on Wednesday.
“He plays the game that way,” said Sox interim manager Chad Tracy. “It’s what he does.”
Still, it seems the injury is impacting him at the plate. He’s hitting .211/.400/.316 in September — showing fight in his at-bats (thus his standout on-base percentage), but rarely driving the ball. His whiff rate (10 percent of swings) is the lowest for any month this year, but he’s rarely been able to drive the ball. His 48 percent ground ball rate is his highest in any month since May.
But to Durbin, the question of whether or how the injury might be affecting him is secondary. His primary concern is simply whether he is positioned to contribute in any way.
“The pain’s gone down drastically since it happened the second time,” Durbin shrugged. “It’s functional.”
Updates on injured trio
Garrett Crochet, who last threw off a mound on Tuesday, worked out at Polar Park in Worcester on Thursday and will continue to throw on flat ground on Friday before the team decides whether to introduce any higher-intensity activities over the weekend.
Tracy said there’s been no discussion about the lefthander pitching in a rehab game for the WooSox this weekend. He didn’t rule out the possibility Crochet could soon face hitters in a live batting practice session, but made clear that there is no known schedule involving the 27-year-old.
“It all depends on how he’s feeling. … He’s been down so long,” said Tracy. “It is day to day. [Friday he’ll] throw, see how he feels, and then determine what the weekend holds.”
Righthander Tyron Guerrero, whose return from shoulder inflammation was delayed slightly by lower back cramps, had a high-intensity throwing session on flat ground. He’s expected to throw off a mound Friday when the Sox open a three-game series at Tampa Bay, a potential prelude to activation later in the weekend. “The shoulder feels great, the arm feels great,” said Guerrero.
Ceddanne Rafaela is increasing (right quad strain) is increasing his agility work but, at this point, there’s “no discernible timeline yet on game action,” according to Tracy. It hasn’t been determined if Rafaela will join the Sox in Tampa.
Oviedo in Worcester
Righthander Johan Oviedo (right elbow strain), pitching in an official game for the first time since March 30, struck out four batters while sitting at 96 miles per hour and touching 99 with his four-seamer in 2⅓ innings in a rehab appearance for the WooSox. He threw 20 of 30 pitches for strikes … Ranger Suarez will start for the Sox on Friday against the Rays, but the Sox have yet to decide who will start the other two games of the series. Payton Tolle, Patrick Sandoval, and Brayan Bello are all considerations … The Red Sox will send two scouts to New York for next week’s four-game Yankees-Rays series, the start of the team’s in-person advance scouting efforts for the postseason.

Video Transcript
What's up, everyone?
Zach Coe here for Roundtable.
Ahead of Tuesday night's loss to the Rangers, Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters that reliever Justin Slayton's season was over after an orthopedic visit revealed degenerative changes in his flexor mass, which required a PRP injection, effectively ending his season.
So obviously, the Red Sox have one of the best bullpens in baseball, backend of Aroldis Chapman, Justin Slayton, and Tayron Guerrero when he returns from the injured list.
But the loss of Slayton is still a really big one for this Red Sox bullpen, especially in the postseason when managers tend to be more aggressive with the hooks on both starters and relievers.
It was a pretty underwhelming season for Slayton when you look at the final line.
It was a 4.60 ERA in 31 1/3 innings.
But he was prone to a couple blowup starts, and that really inflated his ERA for much of the season.
It'll be interesting to see how Tracy's able to piece together the bullpen in Slayton's absence.
Of course, like I said, you have the backend pretty solidified with Tayron Guerrero handling the seventh, Garrett Whitlock in the eighth to All-Star Aroldis Chapman, who's been one of the best closers in baseball over the last two seasons.
But it's how you get to them that I really have some concerns about, and there are plenty of guys that are available to fill that role, but it's whether or not they'll be able to capitalize on their opportunities.
First one being Greg Weiser.
I wrote about it a little bit earlier, but ever since he was recalled from his brief demotion to Triple-A, he's been incredible for the Red Sox, stepping up as they lost guys like Whitlock to an IL stint, Slayton, who landed on the IL shortly after Whitlock, and most recently Guerrero.
There's also Tanner Houk, who's working his way back from Tommy John surgery he underwent last year.
He's gonna try to make a return in a bullpen capacity for the last week of the season.
And then there's the big wild card of it all in Garrett Crochet, who continues to throw side sessions as he tries to get back in a relief role for the postseason.
He's been on the injured list since April 29th with left shoulder inflammation.
So any of those guys are more than capable of stepping up and filling that role.
It's just gonna be about whether or not they're, one, healthy enough to go out there and throw on a near nightly basis like the team might need them to in the postseason, and two, whether or not they're gonna be productive enough.
Obviously, with Houk, he's coming back from Tommy John surgery, and typically you see guys be a little bit wild with their control when they first come back from Tommy John.
We saw it in Houk's first relea-- We saw it in his first rehab appearance with Portland.
He walked two guys, and a run scored as a result.
But it's been a little bit better, since then in the two appearances following that.
So we'll see if that is something that he can shake.
And then Crochet, he's just We haven't seen him in so long, it's tough to say whether or not he's gonna be as effective as he once was.
And even if he isn't able to get to the 2025 Cy Young runner-up caliber, can he at least give you enough to kind of bridge that gap between the starter and to the backend of your bullpen?
And then there's kind of a wild card in it all, and a bit of a forgotten man in Johan Oviedo, who obviously has electric stuff, but he's made only one appearance in a Red Sox uniform before landing on the IL with right elbow inflammation.
So he's planning on making a rehab appearance with Triple-A Worcester on Thursday night, and then they'll figure out the next steps with him.
But Red Sox have plenty of options to fill that void left behind by Slayton.

Originally viewed as one of the favorites to start the season in the Opening Day rotation, Red Sox right-hander Johan Oviedo wound up making just one appearance out of the bullpen before going on the shelf with a right elbow strain.
Now after missing nearly the entire season, Oviedo may finally be nearing a return.
Oviedo began a rehab assignment at Triple-A Worcester on Thursday, throwing 2 1/3 innings for the WooSox in his first game action since late March.
The 28-year-old threw 30 pitches, 20 for strikes, while allowing one run on two hits and a walk while striking out four. Oviedo allowed an RBI double with one out in the top of the second before striking out the final three batters he faced.
More encouragingly, Oviedo’s fastball averaged 95.9 mph and topped out at 98.5, a sizable jump from the 92-93 he averaged earlier in the season.
Originally acquired last winter from the Pittsburgh Pirates as part of the Jhostynxon Garcia trade, Oviedo was initially expected to provide rotation depth as a possible high-ceiling power arm. Oviedo had previously missed extensive time due to Tommy John surgery, but finished his last season in Pittsburgh strong with a 3.57 ERA and 42 strikeouts over nine starts down the stretch.
The righty entered spring as one of the favorites for the No. 5 rotation spot, but after some promising early starts began showing signs of wear. The last rotation spot wound up going to Connelly Early, with Oviedo making the team as a reliever, and he made one appearance against the Houston Astros on March 30, allowing four runs over 3 2/3 innings.
Oviedo has been on the injured list ever since, but now he could be a dark horse candidate for the Red Sox playoff roster along with Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet, who are also working their way back from extended injury absences.
Upcoming starters
Ranger Suarez will start Friday’s series opener against the Tampa Bay Rays, but the Red Sox’s other starters remain to be determined. Payton Tolle would normally be in line to start Saturday but Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters in Texas on Thursday that the club is still deciding how it wants to handle the weekend.
Brayan Bello, who was limited to 19 pitches over 1 2/3 innings on Tuesday, would presumably be a candidate to start one of this weekend’s games.

The Boston Red Sox made one of the very best moves in baseball for the 2026 season, despite the fact that some fans didn't initially believe in the deal.
While searching for a No. 2 starter last offseason, Boston turned to the St. Louis Cardinals and swung a deal for three-time All-Star Sonny Gray. With the Red Sox searching for another elite starter, some wondered if Gray was better suited for a mid-to-back of the rotation spot, rather than the No. 2 spot for a club with World Series aspirations. He has more than delivered and has been Boston's best starter all season. Gray's going to get Cy Young Award votes and Boston should do what it can to try to keep him in town beyond the 2026 season. If he plays, he'll cost a pretty penny. MassLive.com's Chris Cotillo reported that some in the industry believe Gray will get a deal in the range of three years and $75 million — or more — if he continues his career.
"As a free agent, Gray’s renaissance season may position him to receive a lucrative deal that some in the industry expect to match or exceed the three-year, $75 million deal the Rangers gave to Nathan Eovaldi two winters ago," Cotillo wrote. "Interestingly, though, Gray has not committed to pitching again in 2027. In a recent interview with The Boston Globe, Gray said he would retire 'in a heartbeat' if his family signaled that he was wanted back home year-round, even if that meant retiring after the end of this year."
The Red Sox Should Do Everything To Keep Sonny Gray
That's actually also the same deal that the Cardinals gave Gray before the 2024 season as well. He inked a three-year, $75 million pact that he's currently in the final year of. After the season, Gray has a $30 million mutual option for the 2027 season with a $10 million buyout. If Boston picks up its end of the buyout and Gray opts out, then the buyout would be forfeited.
Gray has pitched well enough in a Red Sox uniform to get paid again — if he keeps pitching. So far this season, he has a 17-5 record, 2.76 ERA and 4.0 wins above replacement in 156 2/3 innings pitched. When it comes to Gray, his age stands out at 36 years old. But it hasn't stopped him yet. The price of pitching has gone up in a big way. A deal with a $25 million annual value, as Cotillo pointed out, would be in the range of guys like Michael King, Sean Manaea, and Eovaldi. It would be just above guys like Aaron Nola, Seth Lugo, Robbie Ray and Luis Severino. Gray has been better than all of these guys so far this season.
When it comes to the Red Sox, there isn't as much pitching depth down in the minors as there once was. Over the last year, Boston has traded guys like Hunter Dobbins, Richard Fitts, Brandon Clarke, Anthony Eyanson and Kyson Witherspoon, among others. Plus, Connelly Early was traded as well.
Garrett Crochet, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suárez, and Jake Bennett are locks for the 2027 rotation. Johan Oviedo is someone who could play a role. Tanner Houck is another guy who could as well. We've seen all season how impactful injuries are to the rotation. You never have enough arms. A dependable veteran like Gray for the next few years should be a necessity. It's no guarantee that he pitches beyond the 2026 season, but if he does, it should be in a Boston uniform.

RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses the potential relievers who could step up and fill the void left behind by Justin Slaten after it was revealed the right-hander was unlikely to return from the injured list in 2026. Be sure to join our FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
After an incredible July that saw the Boston Red Sox go 21-4, ultimately saving their season and propelling them into postseason position, the team has given key contributors time on the injured list to address lingering injuries. Among the players placed on the IL was right-handed reliever Justin Slaten, who was dealing with right elbow soreness.
After initially expecting to miss the minimum of 15 days or somewhere close to it, the 29-year-old continued to experience soreness as he began throwing progressions, leading the team to shut him down each time. On Tuesday, interim manager Chad Tracy announced that Slaten received a PRP injection to treat "degenerative changes in his flexor mass," ending his season.
With Slaten set to miss the remainder of the year, the pressure is on these pitchers to help bridge the gap between the starter and All-Star closer Aroldis Chapman:
Tyron Guerrero
Guerrero was expected to be activated off the injured list ahead of Wednesday night's loss to the Texas Rangers, but tightness in his lower back led the team to delay his activation. Still, though, upon his activation, Guerrero will become one of the primary seventh-inning options for Tracy to turn to.
The 35-year-old flamethrower has been an incredible find for Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow, posting a 3.26 ERA in 38.2 innings in 2026. However, he hit a rough patch before landing on the IL, allowing eight earned runs in his last 13.2 innings. Boston will need him to return to the pitcher he was for the first 38.2 innings of his season, when he posted a 2.16 ERA.
After not allowing a single earned run in his first 10 appearances after being dealt to Boston at the trade deadline, the 28-year-old lefty has struggled in his last six outings, allowing five earned runs, including three in a blow-up appearance in Wednesday's loss.
Miller told reporters after the loss that he was working through a mechanical issue that led to the struggles. However, he is the primary left-handed high-leverage arm before Chapman, so the team will need him to get those issues squared away ahead of what's likely to be a Wild Card-round matchup against a New York Yankees lineup that's lefty-heavy.
No single pitcher has stepped up more for the Red Sox as they shuffled Garrett Whitlock, Slaten, and Guerrero on the injured list than Weissert. After a brief demotion to Triple-A Worcester on Aug. 7, Weissert returned to the big leagues on Aug. 13, taking Whitlock's spot on the active roster, and has been lights out ever since. In 10.2 innings since being recalled, the 31-year-old right-hander has allowed only two earned runs on 12 hits, striking out 14 and walking only four.
Weissert figures to be the leader in the clubhouse to take over Slaten's role in the bullpen.
A trio of injured options
The Red Sox have several pitchers looking to return from the injured list before the end of the regular season who could factor into the team's playoff push, including 2025 Cy Young Award runner-up Garrett Crochet, 2024 All-Star Tanner Houck, and Johan Oviedo.
Crochet
The 27-year-old ace has thrown four bullpen sessions since restarting a throwing progression on Aug. 3, with his most recent outing, a 30-pitch up-and-down session on the Fenway Park mound, coming on Tuesday afternoon. While Crochet, if healthy enough to appear in games, will almost certainly be on the postseason roster, he is expected to make multi-inning appearances rather than one-inning spurts like Slaten had been used, making him a valuable weapon but an imperfect replacement.
Houck
The now-30-year-old right-hander is attempting to return to the Boston staff in a "Swiss Army knife" role after undergoing Tommy John surgery in August 2025. Houck has already made three rehab appearances with both Double-A Portland and Triple-A Worcester, allowing two earned runs on one hit, walking four, and striking out seven in 4.2 innings. He is expected to return to Worcester on Saturday for a 40-50 pitch outing before potentially rejoining the Red Sox.
Though what exactly Houck can contribute after being out of major league action since May 2025 remains to be seen.
Oviedo
A bit of a forgotten man in the 2026 Red Sox season is the 28-year-old right-hander, who made only one appearance before landing on the injured list on April 3 with right elbow inflammation. Oviedo will make his first rehab appearance Thursday night with Worcester before deciding on next steps; at this point, the risk likely outweighs the reward of making the postseason roster.
Tracy, Breslow, and the rest of Boston's decision makers will have 10 games to make their final decisions on how exactly the postseason roster will look, and who will replace Slaten's high-leverage innings.
Up next for the Sox
The Red Sox will look to avoid the sweep at the hands of the Texas Rangers in Thursday's series finale from Globe Life Field. Sonny Gray (17-5, 2.76 ERA) gets the start for Boston opposite Tyler Alexander (5-2, 3.38 ERA) for Texas. First pitch is set for 8:05 p.m. ET.

When Erik Miller on September 16 took the mound in front of the Texas Rangers, it didn't take long for things to go awry. Miller's command has never been perfect, but something was definitely off in Arlington, Texas.
It took only three pitches for the big lefty to plunk Corey Seager, and he walked Jake Burger two batters later. On his lone pitch to Brandon Nimmo, the former New York Met knocked a game-changing RBI double to center field, and things crumbled from there.
Ezequiel Duran's two-RBI single, which gave the Rangers a three-run lead, was the last at-bat of the inning before Miller was spared by Adley Rutschman catching Duran stealing. The outing was Miller's worst since he joined the Boston Red Sox at the trade deadline — he allowed three runs on two hits, a walk and a hit batter with one strikeout.
The outing against the Rangers was the second one in as many games that has given Miller trouble. On September 13 against the Kansas City Royals, Miller lasted just a third of an inning after conceding two walks and a fielder's choice. Garrett Whitlock entered after him and gave up a single, but the Royals' lone run of the game was charged to Miller.
Red Sox need Erik Miller to right recent command issues as soon as possible to be right for postseason
After his appearance in Texas, Miller made a concerning statement about his recent struggles. It could be a disastrous sign for Boston's October bullpen.
"Kinda working through some stuff right now," Miller said. "There's some stuff I'm trying to clean up a little bit on the mechanical side. I mean, at some point throughout the year, stuff crops up. I had been doing really well and there are some bad habits I'm kinda falling back into so, yeah, just gotta work through it, gotta get back to what I was doing and go from there."
Miller has been one of Boston's biggest relief weapons since the trade deadline. The Red Sox need him in his best shape all the more with Tyron Guerrero on the injured list and after the announcement that Justin Slaten's season has ended.
Before his shaky command popped up, Miller had done a solid job at limiting free passes, one of the major concerns from his tenure with the Giants. Over his 12 outings in August (including one with the Giants) Miller allowed three walks and a hit batter (0.943 WHIP). Through five outings in September, he's up to six walks and a hit batter (2.077 WHIP). The combination of fatigue and decreased command will make for a brutal outcome for Boston.
Thankfully, the Red Sox are expecting some relief reinforcements for the playoff run. Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet are working toward returns in long relief. But having them plus prime Miller would be the best outcome.
The Red Sox must work more closely with Miller to address his mechanical issue, whatever it is. Over his last two outings, he's served up damaging pitches or free passes, and that won't get Boston far in October, especially given the fatigue its rotation has been showing.

Good morning! Last night, Jake Bennett was unable to hold the Rangers in check during the team's 7-3 loss in Texas. Some of his numbers look good (seven strikeouts against just one walk), but he also surrendered eight hits in just 4.2 innings, which did in his evening.
With just ten games left in the season, the question now becomes how should the Sox use Bennett going forward? With some combination of Sonny Gray, Payton Tolle and Ranger Suarez likely to get lined up in a best of three Wild Card Series, do you just hold Bennett on the sidelines and hope he gets to come back into the fold as a fourth starter in the ALDS or even ALCS? Or do you start transitioning him to some sort of relief role?
It's a bit of an awkward moment for Bennett. He's been getting knocked around during his last two outings while Suarez is seemingly getting locked in. It almost certainly cuts him out of the Wild Card rotation, and if the Sox get some combination of Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck and Tyron Guerrero back to add to Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock and Erik Miller in the bullpen, Bennett largely gets squeezed out of relevance.
So how do you want him used? Do those six shutout innings Bennett threw against the Yankees back on August 29th make you want the Sox to find a role for him if they play New York? Do you think he's just a young pitcher who looks out of gas and want to hide him until the team needs a fourth starter?
Use this space to talk about Bennett and the rest of the difficult upcoming pitching staff decisions, and, as always, be good to one another.

When the Boston Red Sox sent former top-prospect Marcelo Mayer to the San Francisco Giants for Erik Miller, CBO Craig Breslow was sending a major signal. This season is about winning, and Miller will be more help with that now.
For a while, the hard-throwing lefty has been exactly that. A major spark out of the bullpen who makes the Red Sox incredibly intimidating on the mound in the late innings. In his first 14 appearances with Boston, Miller gave up just two runs.
The last two games have been more of a struggle for Miller, though. In 1.1 innings, he’s given up four runs. That includes three runs in Wednesday’s rough loss to the Texas Rangers, which was good enough for Miller to earn a loss.
Boston Red Sox RP Erik Miller Opened Up on Struggles
Following Wednesday’s loss, Erik Miller faced the media following the game. There, he explained that his main issue on Wednesday was that he had control issues. Those control issues put him in bad counts, which made him predictable.
“Just not doing what I’ve been doing well,” Erik Miller said. “Just not getting ahead of guys. Getting behind. Falling into hitters’ counts… Guy knows what’s coming, it usually doesn’t end well. Just kind of working through some stuff right now.”
Red Sox fans and media both noticed Miller saying that he’s working through some stuff. Luckily, that doesn’t mean an injury. It’s more a reference to letting his mechanics get away from him.
“Yeah. Some stuff I’m trying to clean up a little. At some point throughout the year, stuff crops up. You’ve been doing really well and some bad habits kind of come up. So, I’ve just got to work through it. Get back to what I was doing and go from there,” Miller said.
The Red Sox need the version of Miller they’ve largely gotten since the trade. He has a 2.87 ERA in Boston, to go along with a 1.277 WHIP and 14.9 strikeouts per nine. That’s in 15.2 innings over 16 appearances.
Garrett Crochet Will Return to the Red Sox as a Reliever
The Red Sox bullpen is set to get a major boost soon. Ace pitcher Garrett Crochet is getting ready to make his return, but it won’t be as a starter. It’ll be as another power lefty for the bullpen to use.
The expectation had been that Crochet won’t be able to make a rehab and would jump back in right as the first-round of the playoffs start. That may not be the case now. It was recently reported that he could be ready even sooner. That means he’ll potentially pitch in the regular season as a kind of rehab.
“The comebacks of potential October contributors like Tanner Houck, Garrett Crochet, Johan Oviedo and others might also be aided by the fact the Red Sox might have a week (or more) to set up for the postseason,” Chris Cotillo of MassLive wrote. “It’s not out of the question that the club has someone like Crochet pitch in one of the final regular season games of the year in what’s effectively a rehab outing at the major league level in a game that matters little in the standings.”
It’s excellent news for the Red Sox. With Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, a healthy Garrett Crochet, and Erik Miller, Boston can feel very confident if they get just five innings from a starter.

"It's not out of the question that the club has someone like Crochet pitch in one of the final regular season games of the year in what's effectively a rehab outing at the major league level in a game that matters little in the standings."
After finishing second in AL Cy Young voting in 2025, 2026 has been a major disappointment for Crochet. He has a 6.30 ERA and hasn't pitched since April 29th, when he originally hit the IL with left shoulder inflammation. He would later also be diagnosed with a lat strain.
When Crochet does return, it won't be in the rotation. He doesn't have time to build up to that. Instead, the Red Sox are going to be using him out of the bullpen. he
Boston Red Sox Ace Garrett Crochet Doesn't Have Time for a Rehab
The reality for Garrett Crochet is that time is running out for a rehab assignment, and he likely won't have time to make one. That's why the Red Sox would likely want to bring him back before a playoff series.
Regardless of if that chance to come back before the postseason happens, however, Crochet is confident in himself.
"Someone brought it up the other day. They were like, isn't that crazy? I'm like, not really," Crochet said on Monday. "I mean, not [to be all] me, me, me, me, but I've done crazy things before. I'm not Joe Schmoe. I've done impressive things. I think that that would be a big ask for some people, but I don't think it's a crazy ask for me."
This isn't entirely new territory for Crochet. In 2020, the Chicago White Sox added him to their postseason roster when he had limited time in live action due to the pandemic and coming out of college. He pitched well in that brief opportunity, throwing 0.2 innings with 2 strikeouts.
The Red Sox Postseason Rotation is Up for Debate
Heading into the postseason, pitching is a strength for the Red Sox. Even with injuries, that much has become obvious. Still, questions remain about the actual rotation in the postseason.
Sonny Gray and Payton Tolle will make starts in a three-game series. That's not up for debate. There is debate about which of the two gets Game One. Then, Game Three is going to be between Ranger Suarez and Jake Bennett. The lean there is certainly for the well-paid Suarez, who is a veteran with postseason success. However, stranger things have happened.
Starters who could be coming back from injury, including Houck and Crochet, are going to be seen as relievers. That's presumably how the Red Sox will also continue to use Brayan Bello and Patrick Sandoval.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox haven't officially clinched a postseason spot, but all signs point toward a Wild Card Series rematch at Yankee Stadium.
Pitching depth was a problem for the Red Sox in last year's playoff meeting with the Yankees. Their ace Garrett Crochet propelled them to victory in Game 1, but Brayan Bello and an inexperienced Connelly Early couldn't get the job done in Games 2 and 3.
This time, Boston's pitching will be a strength. Veteran right-hander Sonny Gray, rookie southpaw Payton Tolle, and veteran lefty Ranger Suarez can go toe-to-toe with most clubs' 1-through-3. The question is, what's the optimal order to put them in for the three-game Wild Card Series?
It's a good problem to have, and there's really no wrong answer. That said, here's our ideal Wild Card Series rotation for Boston as it looks to avenge last year's crushing defeat:
Justin Leger
Game 1: Sonny Gray
Gray isn't the "sexy" pick. That would be the mustached man I have starting Game 2.
But in what's sure to be an electrifying environment at Yankee Stadium, I want a dependable veteran on the mound to begin the series. I want Mr. Consistency.
All season long, Gray has fit that description.
Gray has a 17-5 record (tied for MLB lead in wins) with a 2.76 ERA through 27 starts. Since Crochet went down with an early-season injury, the 36-year-old has stepped up as the Red Sox' de facto ace with 18 quality starts (tied for seventh in MLB).
Unlike Tolle, Gray has plenty of experience pitching at Yankee Stadium. He's had his fair share of rough starts there throughout his 14-year career, especially during his brief stint with New York, but he was solid there earlier this season with three earned runs across 6.1 innings pitched in a 5-3 victory. In his other start against the Yankees at Fenway Park, he took a no-hitter into the eighth inning.
It'll be an uphill battle for the Red Sox regardless of who's on the mound, because Cy Young frontrunner Cam Schlittler will be poised to shut down Boston's bats yet again. Still, Gray can be counted on to give the Sox a chance to win, and if they lose, they'll have great options to lean on in Games 2 and 3.
Game 2: Payton Tolle
If Tolle is named the Red Sox' Game 1 starter, I won't complain. I'd be slightly concerned that his 0.1 IP in last year's Wild Card Series marks his only experience pitching at Yankee Stadium, but that isn't worth panicking about. He seems built for the bright lights.
Tolle looked sharp in both of his starts against the Yankees at Fenway this season. During his first outing in April, the 23-year-old allowed just one run on three hits across six innings. In his second start against them in June, he carried a perfect game into the sixth inning, finishing with no runs and just one hit allowed over seven innings pitched.
Those were two of many outings this season in which Tolle has looked like an ace. He'll have to perform like one throughout Boston's postseason run, and if he gets the ball in Game 2, he might be counted on to keep Boston's season alive.
Game 3: Ranger Suarez
If it comes down to a do-or-die Game 3, I feel great about Ranger Suarez taking the mound. The 31-year-old veteran has the postseason pedigree with an impressive 1.48 ERA in 11 career appearances (eight starts) with the Philadelphia Phillies.
Suarez endured a second-half slump but has looked more like himself in his last two outings. After tossing seven shutout innings against the Baltimore Orioles on Sept. 4, he allowed just one run across seven innings while striking out eight Kansas City Royals hitters on Saturday. This is the version of Suarez the Red Sox expected to get when they signed him to a five-year, $130 million contract in the offseason.
If Suarez struggles, the Red Sox will have the luxury of an elite bullpen to lean on. Brayan Bello has been an excellent bulk option since reverting to a relief role. Jake Bennett could be a legitimate weapon out of the 'pen as well, along with Crochet if he returns in time from his injury.
Mitchael Hurley
Game 1: Payton Tolle
I'm not opposed to statistics influencing baseball decisions. I rely on statistics more than I should.
But in this case, I don't think they matter. If you've watched the Red Sox this year, it could not be more clear that Payton Tolle is very much the heart and soul of this team. And the idea of sending him out onto the mound at Yankee Stadium with the whole baseball world watching just feels like the obvious choice.
If the Red Sox are going to win a series like this one, they're going to need to be the team with more energy. Nobody would bring more juice to the mound than Tolle. If he can step onto the field on a rainy Sunday four hours after first pitch was scheduled and instantly deliver an immaculate inning in the first, it's frightening to think what type of energy he can bring to a Game 1 start.
The Yankees have struggled against him this year, but even if they hadn't, I've gotta send Tolle to the mound for Game 1.
Game 2: Sonny Gray
In another year, in another circumstance, the 36-year-old Sonny Gray would be in line to win his first career Cy Young Award.
Of course, Cam Schlittler, the Yankees' presumed Game 1 starter, has wrecked any and all Cy Young debate with his sterling season in New York. Still, Gray is having one of the best seasons of his 14-year career, and he has to pitch in this series.
He did allow a pair of homers in his lone start at Yankee Stadium this season, and he's given up 22 homers in 23 appearances there in his career. With the short porch looming and the crowd always looking to erupt, that would be my concern.
But Gray's been great all year, he's been great down the stretch, and the Red Sox will ensure that he's properly rested for this one.
Game 3: Ranger Suarez
Would it look bad if the Red Sox potentially lost the series in two games and never sent Ranger Suarez and his 1.48 postseason ERA to the mound? It sure would.
But given the years that Tolle and Gray have had, I think the Red Sox could live with it.
There is some concern that he got rocked in the Bronx on Aug. 30 (six earned runs in 5.1 innings), but he also allowed one run in six innings in his first start at Yankee Stadium earlier in the season.
Considering the Red Sox had to send rookie Connelly Early out there in Game 3 a year ago to make his fifth career start, the team is clearly in a much better position if another Game 3 awaits them in the Bronx.

Alex Cora said Braiden Ward would be a factor in October.
The Boston Red Sox outfield depth took a major hit ahead of last Friday’s series opener against the Kansas City Royals as the team placed Eli White on the 10-day injured list with a right foot ligament injury, with no timetable for his return. The 32-year-old outfielder not only filled in admirably for the injured Ceddanne Rafaela, but was also slated to play an important role on the postseason roster as the fourth outfielder and pinch runner off the bench. With White now unlikely to return before the postseason, could the Red Sox turn to spring-training standout Braiden Ward to fill the role?
About Ward
The Red Sox acquired Ward in an offseason deal with the Colorado Rockies in exchange for left-handed reliever Brennan Bernardino. The 27-year-old outfielder became one of the biggest storylines of Red Sox spring training, seeing ample playing time as many of Boston's outfield options, including Roman Anthony, Wilyer Abreu and Rafaela, represented their countries in the World Baseball Classic. In 27 Grapefruit League games, Ward hit .378/.509/.444/.953 while stealing 19 bases, setting a single-season spring training record. Ward's dynamic speed caught the eye of now-former manager Alex Cora, who told reporters on several occasions that the 27-year-old would be a factor come October.
After missing the team's opening-day roster amid an already crowded outfield, Ward spent the entire 2026 season in Triple-A Worcester. In 107 games with the WooSox, Ward hit just .238/.356/.355/.711 but set a record for most stolen bases in a single season for a Red Sox Triple-A club with 58 and counting.
There's just one problem...
While Ward seems like a slam-dunk option to fill White's role on the postseason roster, it is not as simple as just recalling him from Triple-A, as he's not on the 40-man roster. The Red Sox 40-man roster currently sits at 39; however, the impending returns of Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck and Johan Oviedo mean the team will have to either designate two players for assignment or move someone to the 60-day IL.
Luckily, there are several candidates for the latter: in White, should he be unable to return for the postseason, designated hitter Masataka Yoshida, utility man Anthony Seigler and reliever Justin Slaten, all of whom appear unlikely to return prior to the end of the season.
Is Ward actually an option?
Interim manager Chad Tracy was asked about the possibility of Ward joining the big-league club during his weekly appearance on WEEI's 'Rich and Ken with Ted Johnson' Show on Wednesday afternoon. "I think that'd be considered for sure," he said when asked about the possibility of Ward joining the big-league team. "It's really hard to predict what a roster could look like, but you definitely can't ignore a 60-stolen-base player," he continued.
However, Tracy cautioned that a pinch runner is a last resort for a team when it's trailing, and teams must consider other options, like whether it would be more valuable to add another right-handed bat or a better defender to the roster. Though Ward does profile as an above-average outfield defender.
Up next for the Sox
After falling 4-2 in Tuesday night's series opener, the Red Sox will look to even up the three-game set with the Texas Rangers in game two of three from Globe Life Field on Wednesday night. Rookie left-hander Jake Bennett (9-7, 3.69 ERA) will get the start for Boston opposite fellow southpaw MacKenzie Gore (8-11, 4.62 ERA) for Texas. First pitch is set for 8:05 p.m. ET.

ARLINGTON -- Tanner Houck continued his rehab assignment with his third Minor League appearance on Tuesday, while Garrett Crochet threw another bullpen session at Fenway Park as both worked toward returning to Boston in relief roles.
The right-hander entered in the seventh and struck out Oliver Dunn looking at a 94.1 mph fastball. He then walked a batter before getting Austin Slater to swing through a 93.6 mph four-seamer and Jack Suwinski to chase an 83.5 mph sweeper.
Houck threw 22 pitches (11 strikes) and reached 94.2 mph with his fastball.
The 30-year-old is expected to make his next appearance on Friday, when he is scheduled for a longer outing in the 45-, 50-pitch range.
“Obviously some swing and miss in there. He has that capability,” interim manager Chad Tracy said ahead of Boston's bout with the Rangers Wednesday. “We all know -- and he said [it] himself, each time he touches the mound, getting his rhythm -- he gets a little bit more comfortable. That's all part of it. The strike-throwing piece and getting command of your pitches.
“So it seems at this point he's at least taking a step forward each time he goes out there, which is good. This next one will be good, being able to see [if he can] replicate that over a longer stretch of pitches.”
Crochet also took another step in his recovery.
The 2025 American League Cy Young Award runner-up threw a 30-pitch bullpen session at Fenway Park. Tracy said the session went well, but as of Wednesday the team did not have much clarity on Crochet’s next steps. He will continue his throwing program this week before the Red Sox re-evaluate him over the weekend.
Crochet has been building up his workload and intensity in recent bullpen sessions. He threw 25 pitches in his previous session Friday, when he incorporated his sweeper and threw his fastball in the 92-93 mph range.

The Red Sox are anticipating some major additions for the postseason, from the long-awaited returns of Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck to the expected activation of Ceddanne Rafaela. A prospect who has yet to debut in the majors could be nearly as impactful.
Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy hinted Wednesday that speedster Braiden Ward could be called up with the postseason looming, after a dominant season on the basepaths in the minor leagues.
Ward, who would have to be added to the 40-man roster, would be eligible for the postseason despite spending the entire year in triple-A Worcester up to this point.
Here's more to know about Ward and his potential call-up.
Who is Braiden Ward?
Tracy told WEEI's "Rich and Ken with Ted Johnson" that Ward could be called up at some point soon. "I think that would be considered, for sure," Tracy said.
Chad Tracy on @richkented talking about potentially calling up Braiden Ward: 'I think that would be considered, for sure.'
— Rob Bradford (@bradfo) September 16, 2026
Ward is 27, which is older than a typical prospect, but he would be coming up for something that can't necessarily be taught: speed. A 16th-round pick out of Washington in 2021, Ward leads triple-A with 58 stolen bases this season and has 269 career minor-league stolen bases in 519 games.
Originally drafted by the Rockies, Ward spent four years in Colorado's system before coming over in return for reliever Brennan Bernardino in a November trade last year.
Pinch-runners can be valuable in the postseason if there is room on the roster, and a foot injury for Eli White could play a role in opening up some space for Ward even if his bat isn't much of a tool the Red Sox can use in October.
Here's a full look at Ward's minor-league stats in 2026.
Braiden Ward Minor League Stats
| Games | AVG | HR | RBI | H | SB | OPS |
| 105 | .238 | 5 | 29 | 87 | 58 | .712 |
Ward hasn't had a strong season offensively, batting .238 without flashing much power, but he still gets on base at more than a 35 percent clip and has a career .386 minor-league on base percentage in part because he has a penchant for getting hit by pitches; Ward has been hit 30 times in 2026.
If the Red Sox give Ward a chance down the stretch, it will be because of his speed. Ward's 58 stolen bases are the most in either triple-A league, and a bit of additional speed on the basepaths in the postseason, when games tend to be lower-scoring, could make a major difference for Boston.

Back in April, the Boston Red Sox's season was going off the rails.
The Red Sox started the season off with a 10-17 record and opted to fire a World Series-winning manager in Alex Cora — plus a handful of other coaches — and take a gamble by turning the reins over to interim manager Chad Tracy. At the time, it seemed like the sky was falling. That's because the losses kept piling up, so much so that the Red Sox were 14 games below .500 at 32-46 on June 25.
At the time, the season looked like a disaster. The Red Sox were trending towards being sellers ahead of the trade deadline, both Roman Anthony and Garrett Crochet were on the Injured List with no end in sight, and it seemed like chief baseball officer Craig Breslow's seat was getting hotter and hotter. But the Red Sox transformed their season and now, with the season winding down, ESPN's Buster Olney reported on Wednesday that the expectation is that both Breslow and Tracy will stay on with Boston beyond the 2026 season.
"But Breslow's vision of a team succeeding with pitching and defense fully manifested, and the Red Sox are closing in on a playoff berth and will likely face the Yankees in the wild-card round, again," Olney wrote. "Manager Chad Tracy has been working under an interim tag all season, something of a head-scratcher; it may be that the two sides talked about the idea of an extension in midseason but set aside the topic for the offseason. But Boston is now expected to retain both Breslow and Tracy."
The Red Sox Are Making The Right Call
This is undoubtedly the right call for the Red Sox at this time.
Let's start with Breslow. Whether you love him or not, he has built a team that can go on a run. Sure, there have been some misses over the last few years. Losing Alex Bregman was a public relations disaster. Not landing one of the big free agent bats, including Kyle Schwarber and Pete Alonso, this past offseason also was a surprise. But there are far more wins under Breslow's belt, than losses.
Sonny Gray is going to get Cy Young Award votes and has been Boston's ace this season. Ranger Suárez was an All-Star. Willson Contreras was an All-Star. Caleb Durbin is the heart and the soul of the 2026 Red Sox. Now, the Red Sox have an All-Star catcher on their hands in Adley Rutschman. Bringing back Mickey Gasper has turned into a game-changing move. And the list goes on. The Red Sox have a roster that can make noise.
On the Tracy front, there was obviously a learning curve to being a big league manager taking over during a season, especially in such a high-profile market, like Boston. He has handled the role with grace and has clearly gotten better as the year has gone on. Plus, it doesn't hurt that the Red Sox went on a historic 15-game winning streak and put together one of the best mid-season turnarounds in MLB history. All in all, these two should both be back in 2026 and it sounds like that will be the reality.

The Boston Red Sox could have a slew of pitching reinforcements returning before the playoffs begin, including Tanner Houck, Garrett Crochet, and maybe even Johan Oviedo and Kutter Crawford. Justin Slaten will not be among them.
Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy on September 15 told reporters (including Tim Healey of The Boston Globe) that Slaten got a PRP injection in his arm to address a flexor issue. His season is over after multiple attempts to ramp up for a rehab assignment and eventual return.
Slaten has been quite injury prone over his three years with the Red Sox. He went on the injured list for the first time this season in early April and didn't return until mid-May. For the second straight year, he'll finish his season with less than 35 innings pitched.
Justin Slaten's season with Red Sox ends after he gets PCP injection for flexor injury
The righty has dabbled in the extremes this season, finishing with a 4.60 ERA over 31.1 innings. In June, Slaten's worst month this year, he allowed nine runs on 17 hits over 11 outings. July was his best, during which he let up just one run on five hits over nine appearances. His WHIP has starkly increased over the past year, from 1.09 in 2025 to 1.37.
When the Red Sox can get Slaten's best, he's one of the biggest threats out of their bullpen. But he's often injured or prone to blowups that keep him from showing the best he can offer. It will be interesting to see his role next season when Boston has more healthy pitching depth it could push to the bullpen.
Red Sox confirm Kristian Campbell's season is over due to foot injury, ending breakout
Kristian Campbell's season has also ended prematurely due to an injury. The outfielder will be out for the rest of the year due to a left foot contusion, according to Tommy Cassell of the Worcester Telegram & Gazette.
The WooSox pulled Campbell from their September 8 game due to the injury. Even before the announcement of his IL stint, it was evident that Campbell's season could be over, as Worcester's last regular season game is on Septembet 20.
Campbell's injury ends a resurgent second half for the 24 year old. He slashed .311/.430/.497 over 51 games after the All-Star break and, had he been healthy, he might've been selected to come up and help the major league team while Ceddanne Rafaela and Eli White are injured.
Romy Gonzalez continues tear following arm injury scare with WooSox
On the same day Campbell was pulled from the WooSox's lineup, Romy Gonzalez was, too. An arm injury led to a week on the shelf for the utility infielder, but he joined the Triple-A lineup again on September 15.
Gonzalez has resumed the tear he was on before his arm flared up. He logged two hits, including a double, in his return and boosted his September slash line to .500/.520/.727 over six games. Gonzalez has hit so well lately that it could be time to call him back up to the major leagues to give Boston's slumping offense a boost.
