This morning, we asked whether the Red Sox were ready to give Romy Gonzalez another chance. From his point of view, he’s ready to go. After acknowledging that his initial rehab was rushed in an attempt to get back on the field, he now says “I’m ready whenever my name’s called… I’ve always been extremely confident in what I can do… I think I’ve showed that over the past two seasons.” (Christopher Smith, MassLive)
Speaking of rehabbing power-hitting infielders, what’s Curtis Mead up to?
I’m not sure “light” tee work at this stage is going to have him ready for the postseason in time, but you never know.
Unfortunately there’s one player who definitely won’t return from injury in time. Justin Slaten, who was initially on the IL with elbow inflammation, has been shut down for the season. Moreover, it looks like the issue might be more serious than initially thought. “There’s some degenerative changes in the flexor mass,” Chad Tracy said. “So that’s substantially different news.” He’ll receive a plasma injection to stimulate healing, and, unfortunately, this sounds like something that could require surgery eventually. (Hayden Bird, Boston.com)
Things are progressing for Garrett Crochet, though. He threw thirty pitches over two simulated innings yesterday. “Everything went well,” Chad Tracy said. “That was the most volume he’s had, so we’ll see over the next couple of days how he feels and go from there.” (Tim Healey, Boston Globe)
Hopefully Crochet can work his way back like Trevor Story, who is well aware that he has doubters amongst the Red Sox fanbase and media. “You see a lot of that stuff, but I really try to channel it into an energy in a way that I can use,” he said. “At the time, I wasn’t trying to pay much attention to it, but people would bring it to me, and I decided how I was going to look at it. I just tried to channel it into when I do come back, and it’s all about the playoffs, and it’s all about winning this thing at the end. That’s where I put my energy and focus.” (Jen McCaffrey, The Athletic)

When the Boston Red Sox made some additions to their starting rotation last winter, they were hoping to rebuild it around ace Garrett Crochet. Little did they know that making those moves would turn out to be monster moves.
After losing out on Alex Bregman in free agency to the Chicago Cubs, Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow pivoted to pitching. He signed left-hander Ranger Suárez of the Philadelphia Phillies. Earlier in the offseason, Breslow acquired veteran Sonny Gray from the St. Louis Cardinals.
That is turning into the biggest offseason addition made by Boston. He is going to finish at least in the top 5 in the American League Cy Young voting, but will be a free agent following the season with an option for 2027. Breslow and Gray will have a decision to make this winter, according to Kerry Miller of Bleacher Report.
Boston Red Sox Facing Sonny Gray Decision This Winter
When decisions are to be made for 2027, Gray has a mutual option of $30 million. Now, whether or not Gray plays next season remains to be seen, according to Alex Speier of the Boston Globe.
“If my family wants me to hang it up, I’ll be done in a heartbeat,” Gray said, per Speier.
If they don’t want him to retire, the Red Sox would love to have him back. He is 17-5 in his first season in Boston with a 2.76 ERA in 27 starts. He has been a workhorse in 156.2 innings with 140 strikeouts. Gray has struggled in recent outings. However, he is still on track to get the ball in Game 1 of the AL wild-card series.
“Even with major money committed to Ranger Suárez and Garrett Crochet in the rotation already, chief baseball officer Craig Breslow will probably pick up the team’s half of the option,” Miller wrote.
“The question is whether Gray will. Considering he’ll pitch next season at 37, he’s probably not going to get more than $30 million for 2027 as a free agent. However, if he declines the option, the Red Sox will owe him a $10 million buyout. So he could collect that buyout, try to get at least $20 million for 2027, and perhaps pursue a multi-year commitment. He has plenty to consider.”
Crochet has been out injured for a majority of this season and is looking for a postseason return. Suárez has been better in his last couple of starts in September.
Boston Red Sox Facing Key Offseason Decision
Gray is scheduled to make his next start on Thursday night against the Texas Rangers in Arlington. Then he’ll get one more next week before his start in the wild-card round. Depending on how far the Red Sox go, all eyes could turn to 2027.
Boston’s rotation next season, if healthy when the season begins, with Gray, could be one of the top ones in the American League. If there is any question as to whether or not Gray has another year left in him, that should have been answered by his 2026 season.
There are some big decisions coming for Breslow this winter. Gray is going to be at the top of that list.

Garrett Crochet is looming over the Boston Red Sox's playoff push, despite the fact that he hasn't taken the hill in a big league game since April 25.
At this point, a new update seems to surface in Crochet's attempted return to game action every few days. And all of them have been positive, to say the least. On Tuesday, Crochet threw another bullpen and tossed his most pitches yet (30) en route back to Boston, per The Boston Globe's Tim Healey.
"Garrett Crochet’s two-inning, 30-pitch bullpen session — his heaviest workload so far — went well today, Chad Tracy said. He’ll rest for a couple of days. Sounds like he still won’t be getting into a Triple-A game before that season ends Sunday," Healey wrote.
Garrett Crochet Is Getting Closer
There's a lot to take away from this update for the big lefty. First and foremost, the fact that he's been able to continue throwing and building up is a huge positive. In his last outing on Friday, Crochet tossed just over 20 pitches and introduced his sweeper into the mix. Now, a few days later, he's up to 30 pitches and also an up-and-down. The up-and-down is important in itself. That's a simulation of game action. If Crochet does return to game action before the 2026 season comes to an end, it's going to be in a bullpen role.
He's not coming back to be the starter Boston fans have seen, but instead hopefully a multi-inning weapon to take the bullpen to an even higher level. Now, the next step is going to be seeing how he reacts to the starting and stopping of the up-and-down. If he comes away feeling good, it will be massive for his chances of a return.
The fact that Healey reported that it doesn't sound like Crochet will pitch in Triple-A before Worcester's season comes to a close isn't shocking. In early September, it was shared that Crochet was trending towards a return for the postseason, even if he doesn't go on a rehab assignment beforehand. So, this already has been an idea out there.
When it comes to Crochet, the biggest thing to watch now is when he will face live batters. That's the next significant step. The second the Red Sox have him facing live hitters, that will be the next big step in his recovery. Crochet is close. He has thrown a handful of bullpens already and now he has an up-and-down under his belt. The Red Sox will begin a Wild Card round series on Sep. 29. That's 13 days away, as of writing. It's still very possible for Crochet to provide some much-needed help for this bullpen.

item.content:encoded:
Over the last few weeks, or so, it has seemed like pretty much every injury update for the Boston Red Sox has been positive.
Garrett Crochet has been throwing, Tanner Houck has been on a rehab assignment and even Curtis Mead has been playing catch, among others. While this is the case, the Red Sox gave a negative update on Wednesday. Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy shared that reliever Justin Slaten is dealing with "degenerative changes in the flexor mass" and is likely done for the 2026 season.
"Slaten, we got ... he went and saw [Dr. Keith Meister] with our medical staff today and there's some degenerative changes in the flexor mass," Tracy said. "So he's going to be down. He's going to get a PRP injection and it's likely going to end his season. So, that's substantially different news, as far as these guys."
Bad News For Boston
This is a brutal blow for Slaten, and the Red Sox's bullpen in general. Slaten is one of the club's key high-leverage guys, but Boston hasn't had him on the mound since Aug. 12. He was initially placed on the Injured List due to right elbow inflammation. He actually started throwing, but he had to be shut down when the same "symptoms" that landed him on the Injured List popped up again.
Slaten had a 4.60 ERA in 36 appearances, but this doesn't tell the full story about why he's a big loss for Boston. In his final 17 appearances of the season, he had a 2.45 ERA and a 19-to-3 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 14 2/3 innings pitched. The first half of the season wasn't great for him, but he had turned things around and looked like the guy Boston hoped it would have out of the bullpen.
The Red Sox have just 11 games left in the 2026 regular season. Losing Slaten hurts Boston's playoff chances. On the bright side, the Red Sox's bullpen could still get better with Houck on a minor league rehab assignment and Garrett Crochet throwing as well. With Slaten likely out for the season, that's one less change Boston will have to make when building the playoff roster. Tyron Guerrero, Crochet, and Houck are all inching their way back. Boston will have to clear three spots to get these guys on the roster. That could be bad news for guys like Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, and Raymond Burgos, among others.
With Slaten likely not coming back, it's one less decision for Boston to make. Of course, it would be better if he were returning, but that isn't the case right now. Unfortunately, Red Sox fans have seemingly seen the last of Slaten for the 2026 season.

item.content:encoded:
Jake Bennett might not be Garrett Crochet, but the 25-year-old rookie has done an admirable job this season filling in for the injured Boston Red Sox ace. In fact, the youngster looked pretty Crochet-like with a 2.64 ERA in the first half, despite relying much less on the strikeout to generate that success.
However, as we race toward October, it's time to start thinking about the postseason rotation, and we could see Bennett as the odd man out. Since August 1, the youngster has made seven starts and posted a 5.26 ERA.
The way he's performed over his last three starts has been interesting. On August 29, he twirled six scoreless innings against the New York Yankees while allowing just three hits. On September 3, he took the ball against the Baltimore Orioles and again went six deep, this time surrendering three runs. The two outings were basically the opposite ends of the spectrum of what we'd consider acceptable for a starter in the playoff rotation.
That Orioles start had a hidden concern, though. Bennett served up two homers, and it would prove prophetic for the next time he took the mound. That came on September 9 against the hapless Los Angeles Angels, who torched him for six earned runs over 5 1/3 innings. Bennett got taken deep three times in the affair and allowed eight balls to be hit over 100 miles per hour. His average exit velo for the start was a whopping 95.6 miles per hour.
At the same time, his chief competition for a spot in the playoff rotation, Ranger Suarez, might be rounding into form. The veteran struggled mightily in August after returning from the groin issue that landed him on the IL back in July, posting a 5.70 ERA for the month.
His lone start of September, though, was vintage Suarez, turning in seven shutout innings while allowing just five hits and a walk and generating a whole lot of soft contact.
If Ranger Suarez can prove he's back, he'll swipe Jake Bennett's spot in the Red Sox's playoff rotation
One start doesn't erase all the concern, but Suarez earned the second All-Star nod of his career thanks to his mostly stellar work in the first half. It's not unreasonable to assume that his string of uninspiring August performances was simply due to him knocking off the rust after being on the IL.
For Bennett, there's an added layer. With 105 innings already on his ledger in the majors and another 39 1/3 frames for the WooSox, he's well past what he's used to. In his first minor league season back in 2023, he pitched 63 frames. He missed the entire 2024 season after undergoing Tommy John surgery, and then came back to throw 75 1/3 innings last season.
Essentially, his 144 1/3 combined innings this year alone are greater than the 138 1/3 inning workload he's carried the last three years combined. He can say that the increased run hasn't affected him, but if the results on the field tell a different story, then that's the likely case.
There are two other factors to consider in the event of a proverbial tie. One, the Red Sox gave Suarez $130 million over the winter for a reason. Contracts shouldn't give an underperforming player a boost over a younger, cheaper option, but if all else is equal, it can help to be the deciding factor.
More importantly, Suarez is experienced in October. During his time with the Phillies, he's thrown 42 2/3 playoff innings and owns a 1.48 postseason ERA. That experience, and more importantly, excellence, matters, especially when it seems that the other option is running out of gas.

ARLINGTON, Texas — For the Red Sox, the vision of contention in 2026 seemed straightforward.
The team’s championship window had been pried open by the presence of a pair of cornerstones, with Garrett Crochet anchoring the rotation and Roman Anthony representing a lineup anchor not only for this year but several seasons to come.
But while the Sox are amid a magic-number countdown to a playoff berth, they’ve done so without Anthony and Crochet for most of the year. Their season has been saved in no small part by players who have emerged from obscurity to play critical roles — with essential contributions coming from Andruw Monasterio, Anthony Seigler, Mickey Gasper, Tsung-Che Cheng, Jahmai Jones, Tyron Guerrero, and more.
“I don’t think anybody had that on the drawing board,” said interim manager Chad Tracy with a chuckle. “They were asked to play a lot, and they produced. And if they didn’t, we were in trouble. It’s a huge piece of the 2026 season, no question.”
Of course, while no one expected the outsized impact of players who began the year as big league backups or in Triple-A, the Sox also took considerable pains to build organizational depth through a variety of transactions.
Whether it was an expanded version of the trade that brought Caleb Durbin from Milwaukee to include Monasterio and Seigler, or waiver claims of Cheng and Gasper, or a minor league deal for Guerrero, the season has been a case study in the notion that perceived little moves can have a huge impact.
“Every move and every decision matters,” said assistant general manager Mike Groopman, who oversees the team’s acquisitions group. “The big ones, whether it’s a larger free agent deal, [or] a larger, more high-profile trade, is naturally going to get a lot of attention.
“I don’t think this is unique to the Red Sox. There are 29 other teams that try to and do a very good job about caring about the ‘little’ things. But I think what we really try to reinforce is … that year over year, around the game, you see things that seem ‘little’ that end up being really impactful and big. [Deals that] seemed like small moves at the outset end up having a much, much larger impact commensurate with what would have been perceived at the time as a ‘larger’ move.”
Players who evolve from theoretical depth to become big league contributors excite numerous corners of an organization. The primary credit for those contributions, of course, belongs with a player, but they still often represent the combined efforts of personnel in scouting who identify the player’s potential contributions, player development personnel who help the player build on preexisting strengths and abilities in the minors, and big league staffers who help the players to perform at the game’s highest level.
Take Guerrero. After brief stints in the big leagues in 2018 and 2019, he’d become a journeyman, shuffling between organizations — and countries — but unable to forge a way back to the big leagues despite elite velocity.
But the Sox — who’d been interested in signing Guerrero before he pitched in the NPB in Japan in 2025 — remained intrigued, thanks in part to strong scouting recommendations from Kento Matsumoto in Japan and Manny Nanita in the Dominican Winter League. After they signed Guerrero to a minor league deal in the offseason, player development officials worked with him on some minor grip changes that unlocked significantly improved command with a sinker that regularly reached triple digits.
Guerrero’s dominance this year in Triple-A (0.92 ERA) essentially forced the Sox to call him up, and the 35-year-old emerged as a late-innings force from late June to late August (before shoulder fatigue led to a bad outing followed by a trip to the injured list), posting a 2.13 ERA over a 23-appearance stretch.
Again, the lion’s share of the credit goes to Guerrero for the work he did to fight his way back to the big leagues. But his emergence embodies the sort of under-the-radar acquisition that helped save the Sox’ season.
“The connection and integration between acquisition and development is really important,” said Groopman. “Guerrero and our [player development] group put a lot of time into [those changes] in the spring and the early season, to get him to a point where he was able to lock in some of these changes and unlock what was super obvious arm talent into something that was translating more consistently onto the major league mound.”
Of course, talent alone doesn’t dictate success once a depth player gets to the big leagues. They must also have the opportunity to contribute — and, in many cases, the freedom to fail while getting their bearings.
Tracy, who spent time with nearly all of this year’s depth contributors in Triple-A at the beginning of the year, has been mindful of creating an environment in which call-ups can contribute.
“I’m in the same boat [as them]. I want the freedom to go manage the game [as a first-time big league manager],” said Tracy. “I need to manage a game and feel like if I do something that doesn’t go right, it’s not the end of the world. If I feel that way, then I want the player to feel like, ‘Hey, if you go out there and play second base today and you make an error, move on to the next play.’
“If the culture becomes, ‘If I make a mistake, then all of a sudden I clam up and I get really tight,’ we’re going to have a problem. So you look at them and say, ‘You’re here for a reason: To go play your game. Don’t worry about making a mistake. Move on to the next pitch, next play.’ And they did that, and they were awesome.”

BOSTON, MASSACHUSETTS – APRIL 08: Garrett Crochet #35 of the Boston Red Sox pitches against the Toronto Blue Jays during the first inning at Fenway Park on April 08, 2025 in Boston, Massachusetts.
Photo by Brian Fluharty/Getty Images
Chad Tracy and the Red Sox know some reinforcements on the mound are coming.
And speaking ahead of Tuesday's loss to the Rangers, Tracy provided the masses with a mixed bag sort of update on those rehabbing arms trying to work their way back to Boston in time for the final push of the regular season and the playoffs.
Beginning with Garrett Crochet, Boston's ace who has been sidelined since late April, things continue to trend in the right direction, according to Tracy.
"Crochet threw today [and] that went well," Tracy said. "Everything went well. We’ll wait and see on the next steps, [but] that was the most volume he’s had, so we’ll see over the next couple of days how he feels and then we’ll go from there.”
Crochet and the Red Sox have outright said that any return to action this season would by all means have to come in a reliever role. Crochet, meanwhile, has even suggested that he could make his return to the roster in the postseason.
Elsewhere on the rehab front, Tanner Houck took his best step yet in what's been an improbable run back into the picture as a legitimate option for the Red Sox.
On the hill for the Woo Sox in what was his third rehab outing (but first in Triple A), Houck allowed one walk and struck out three batters in one inning out of the bullpen. Houck is now up to seven strikeouts and has surrendered just one hit (but four walks) over 4.2 innings of work through three games between Portland and Worcester.
The hard-throwing Tyron Guerrero, meanwhile, is eligible to return from the injured list on Wednesday. Guerrero has been on the injured list since Sept. 1 with right shoulder inflammation, and could be a hugely important piece of the puzzle for Boston down the stretch given his dominant stretches earlier in the year.
But Tracy's seemingly endless parade of updates also came with some bad news, as he revealed that the club will be without Justin Slaten for the rest of the season.
Justin Slaten #63 of the Boston Red Sox pitches against the Detroit Tigers at Comerica Park.
"There was some degenerative changes in the flexor mass, so he's going to be [shut] down," Tracy said of Slaten, who met with Dr. Keith Meister, and his status moving forward. "He's going to get a PRP injection and likely going to end his season."
Slaten, who has not pitched since has not pitched since the club's Aug. 12 loss to Toronto, had recently started throwing from 90 feet before the shutdown. Slaten had really turned it on over his last 14 appearances prior to landing on the shelf, too, with 14 strikeouts and a 2.19 ERA in 12.1 innings of work before his season ended.
Fresh off a 4-2 loss to the Rangers on Tuesday but firmly in control of the second wild card in the American League, the Red Sox have another 11 games to get Crochet, Houck, Guerrero, and whoever else up to speed before the postseason begins.

One miserable inning was enough to put the Red Sox in a hole. A pair of missed opportunities prevented them from climbing out of it.
Patrick Sandoval endured a brutal 44-pitch second inning in which the Rangers scored four times, and the Red Sox repeatedly came up empty with runners on base in a 4-2 loss Tuesday night at Globe Life Field.
Boston (82-69) opened its final road trip of the regular season with a loss and fell to 7-6 in September. The Red Sox did, however, move another step closer to securing a postseason berth after Toronto was routed by Detroit, reducing Boston’s magic number to five.
Any potential celebration will have to wait until after the Red Sox leave Texas. Even if Boston wins the final two games of the series, Toronto is off Thursday and would remain mathematically alive entering Friday.
Sandoval’s night began when he struck out the first four Rangers he faced before everything unraveled in a second inning that seemed as though it might never end.
With two outs, Brandon Nimmo and Ezequiel Duran delivered hard-hit singles at 106.3 mph and 105.3 mph, respectively. Elias Díaz followed by pulling a two-run double into left field to give Texas a 2-0 lead.
Sandoval never recovered walking former Sox catcher Danny Jansen and Justin Foscue before Corey Seager dropped a bloop single into shallow left, just beyond the reach of Trevor Story, allowing two more runs to score. By the time Sandoval finally escaped, he had thrown 44 pitches in the inning and Boston trailed 4-0.
Sandoval lasted just 2 2/3 innings and saw his ERA climb to 4.99.
“They drug at bats out on him,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters postgame. “It looked like he was going to get out of there with Diaz, that was a long at bat, I think one of those pitches was close and then he hits the double in the corner and it was just a struggle, we just couldn’t get out of the inning.”
The left-hander’s return from injury provided Boston with some needed innings after he was activated July 9, and he delivered several quality outings along the way. But with the postseason approaching, his place on the October roster has become increasingly uncertain.
Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, Payton Tolle and Jake Bennett are ahead of him in the rotation picture, while Brayan Bello has found success in a bulk role. Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck are also attempting to return before the postseason.
Patrick Sandoval strikes out the side in the 1st.
Justin Foscue made him throw 9 pitches to start the game. Needed 19 total to finish the inning. pic.twitter.com/qpUpDLA5Rc
Sandoval will have time to try and clean things up, but it’s looking as if the Red Sox are better suited with the lefty as a spectator when they inevitably travel to the Bronx.
Boston’s offense quickly cut the deficit in half against Jacob deGrom.
Nick Sogard jumped on a pitch in the third and sent it down the right-field line for a two-run homer, pulling the Red Sox within 4-2.
Sogard didn’t hit his first major league homer until his 322nd plate appearance Aug. 19. He has now hit five in his last 99 plate appearances, all coming over a 24-game span.
The versatile infielder contributed in other ways, too. Sogard perfectly executed a sacrifice bunt in the fifth to move two runners into scoring position and later made an athletic play to complete a 1-4-3 double play.
But the Red Sox couldn’t capitalize on their opportunities against deGrom. The Texas right-hander held Boston to three hits and struck out eight over five innings while maintaining a fastball around 97 mph.

The 2026 season has been, for the most part, an injury-plagued loss for Crochet, who made his first six starts before getting shut down with left shoulder inflammation that regressed when he made his first attempted comeback in late May.
But the beauty of all this is that Crochet can wash away the sour taste of missing most of the season by getting back as a reliever in time for the most important games.
After that setback at the end of May, it took Crochet three months just to be cleared to throw off the mound again.
Now that he’s been able to do so three times, and is scheduled for a fourth bullpen session at Fenway Park on Tuesday, there is legitimate hope he can be on the roster when the Red Sox open their postseason on Sept. 29 -- likely at Yankee Stadium.
This time, assuming he makes it back, Crochet will be cast in a much different role, but one that can still be impactful.
Figuring you have questions about how and when Crochet fits in, here are some answers.
Can Crochet make it back before the regular season ends?
It’s not impossible. His next key step after graduating from bullpen sessions will be to face hitters. That could happen as soon as this weekend, depending on what the club decides after Tuesday’s session.
Ideally, when it comes to Crochet’s situation, the Triple-A season would go a little longer. But, alas, it ends on Sunday.
It seems more likely Crochet will throw live batting practice and/or some type of simulated game rather than getting into a Minor League game, perhaps doing so multiple times.
Would this leave time for one tune-up before the regular season ends on Sept. 27? Perhaps, but not necessarily.
Would Crochet be thrown right into the fire of the playoffs?
What if there isn’t time for Crochet to pitch in any type of game setting before the Wild Card Series starts? Would the Red Sox still put him on the roster?
Well, if he’s throwing up to his capabilities, the answer is absolutely yes.
“It's Garrett Crochet,” said Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy. “If Garrett Crochet looks like Garrett Crochet and he's healthy and able to go out there and pitch, and it looks like him? Yeah, that helps any team.”
What would Boston’s bullpen cast look like with Crochet in the mix?
In a word, dominant. Through their first 150 games of the season entering Tuesday, Boston’s bullpen has a 3.11 ERA, best in the Majors. That’s without Crochet.
Now, add Crochet and possibly 2024 Tanner Houck, who is on a Minor League rehab assignment in his return from Tommy John surgery, and Tracy’s relief crew could have a succession of pitchers with nasty stuff.
At 38 years old, lefty Aroldis Chapman continues to be a force. He has one of the best eighth-inning setup men in the game in front of him in righty Garrett Whitlock. Tyron Guerrero, the righty with triple-digit heat, is due back in the next couple of days after missing the last couple of weeks with right shoulder inflammation. Power lefty Erik Miller has been tremendous since he was acquired at the Aug. 3 Trade Deadline.
Brayan Bello, who hasn’t had much success has a starter this season but has been largely stellar in relief, is another weapon. Add Crochet and Houck to those five pitchers and the Sox would have bullpen depth that would be the envy of most teams.
How would the Sox use Crochet?
The beauty of Crochet is that he could work out of a hybrid role, meaning he could be available for whichever part of the game Tracy needs him most.
Keep in mind that Crochet was a relief pitcher not just in college at Tennessee, but also for the White Sox before being converted to a starting role in ‘24. He has experience working in the early, middle and late part of games.
Thinking outside the box, the Sox could even deploy Crochet as an opener if the occasion called for it, given his experience starting games.
“He'd have plenty of comfort opening if you wanted to go that route," Tracy said. "He pitched out of the 'pen. So if you need him to come in the middle innings of a game, a two-inning pocket, I'm sure he'd have comfort doing that, too."

item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas — Among a series of minor injury updates offered by Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy on Tuesday came some finality on one key reliever. Righty Justin Slaten, after further assessment by a renowned orthopedist in the Dallas area, won’t return to the Red Sox this year.
Slaten visited Dr. Keith Meister on Monday’s off day and testing on his injured elbow revealed “degenerative changes in the flexor mass,” according to Tracy. Slaten is set for a platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection that is all but certain to rule out his return in 2026.
“It’s a big loss,” Tracy said, “at least now, with the finality of knowing we can’t have him back.”
Slaten was placed on the injured list with elbow inflammation in mid-August and dealt with recurring discomfort as he tried to resume throwing. As of the weekend, he was completely shut down from his progression. Now, he will receive the injection and rest in hopes of getting the issue fixed for 2027.
“Probably just means a chronic thing over time, but I’m speculating there,” Tracy said. “I just know that the conservative course of action is PRP, then he’s gonna rehab and go from there. Because of that, it’s probably going to cost him the rest of the season.”
Slaten appeared in 36 games for the Red Sox this year, posting a 4.60 ERA as a mid-relief option ahead of setup man Garrett Whitlock and closer Aroldis Chapman. For the third straight season, injuries were a big part of Slaten’s season. In 2024, he missed about six weeks due to elbow inflammation in July and August. Last season, he was out from June 1 to August 28 with a balky shoulder. This year, he suffered an oblique strain in early April and missed 31 games, then hit the IL again for the final six weeks.
Mead takes step forward
For the first time since having his left wrist broken by a wayward pitch in West Sacramento on July 27, Curtis Mead will do some offensive work in Boston on Wednesday. According to Tracy, Mead — who is out of a cast and has been doing defensive and baserunning drills for weeks — will hit lightly off a tee as he begins his swing progression.
“Mead will begin, tomorrow, introducing tee work,” Tracy said. “Obviously, we’ve talked a lot about the defensive stuff, being able to catch throws and he’s been doing that. Tomorrow, he’ll start doing some tee work with a light bat and then just kinda progress from there.”
With just 12 games left in the regular season, Mead is in a race against the clock to be fully ready for game action, a reality he acknowledged just last week. But it’s still notable that he’s ready to start taking swings in anticipation for potentially returning during the postseason if the Red Sox make a run.
Crochet throws again at Fenway
Left-hander Garrett Crochet took another small step toward a late-season return Tuesday, throwing a two-inning “up-and-down” bullpen (that includes a break simulating a between-inning breather) at Fenway Park. That session came four days after a one-inning high-intensity bullpen on the same mound.
“That went well,” said Tracy. “Everything went well.”
The next step for Crochet might be facing hitters in a live batting practice/simulated game setting but it’s very unlikely he’ll be ready to pitch in a rehab game before Triple-A Worcester’s season ends Sunday. A more likely scenario involves him getting into a simulated game or two and then making a relief appearance late in next week’s final homestand of the year.
“We’ll wait and see on the next steps,” Tracy said. “That was the most volume he’s had, so we’ll see how he feels and go from there.”
Guerrero close to return, Kelly has setback
Right-hander Tyron Guerrero, out since September 1 with shoulder inflammation, is with the Red Sox in Arlington and is expected to be activated before Wednesday’s game. Lefty Raymond Burgos and righty Wyatt Olds are the two leading candidates to be sent down as Guerrero takes a roster spot.
“We’ll see how everything goes with that today,” Tracy said.
The return of Guerrero will give the Red Sox another high-octane option at the end of a bullpen that also includes lefty Erik Miller, Whitlock and Chapman (and won’t have Slaten for the rest of the year).
One reliever who won’t contribute the rest of the way is righty Zack Kelly, who has been out since early July with a stress reaction in the olecranon (bone at the tip of the elbow). Kelly had been throwing live BP sessions in Fort Myers and was close to a rehab outing but had a setback last week and will undergo updated imaging this week.
Rafaela progressing
Center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela (right quad strain) has said his goal is to rejoin the Red Sox for this weekend’s series against the Rays and that is still in play. He’s back in Boston and going through strength tests on his leg while ramping up his running program.
“Started to increase running volume today,” Tracy said. “Nothing new to report there. He’ll continue to do that over the next 2-3 days and we’ll see where he’s at.”
The Red Sox could be careful with Rafaela and welcome him back early next week when the Guardians are at Fenway Park.
Houck, Oviedo on track for rehab outings
Right-hander Tanner Houck is pitching for the WooSox at Polar Park on Tuesday as planned. His outing was planned as a shorter relief outing (he entered in the seventh, following six strong innings for starter Jedixson Paez) and he’s expected to make another appearance over the weekend in a longer stint on the mound.
Right-hander Johan Oviedo is still on track to make a rehab start in Worcester on Thursday.

item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas — Reliever Justin Slaten’s season is all but over after the discovery of a “degenerative” arm issue, Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said Tuesday before a 4-2 loss to the Rangers.
Before the series opener against the Rangers, Slaten went with team medical staff to visit Keith Meister, a highly regarded orthopedic and sports medicine surgeon based in Arlington.
Meister diagnosed the reliever, who had been out with what the club called right elbow inflammation, with a more serious problem.
“There’s some degenerative changes in the flexor mass,” Tracy said. “So that’s substantially different news.”
The flexor is in the forearm and connects to the elbow. Slaten will receive an injection of platelet-rich plasma, which is supposed to stimulate healing. Tracy called it “the conservative course of action.”
Already, with Slaten’s pain lingering well beyond what the Red Sox figured would be a brief shutdown period when he went on the injured list on Aug. 16, he was trending toward not having time to return this season.
“This maybe adds some finality to the fact,” Tracy said. “We were already operating that way, but you still held out hope. ‘Hey, if it can turn the corner and [with] what he’s able to do out of that bullpen. . . . So yeah, it’s a big loss — at least now, the finality of knowing we can’t have it back.”
For Slaten, who turned 29 on Tuesday, it is another in a string of injuries that have limited his impact. Since reaching the majors in 2024, he has missed time because of elbow, shoulder, and oblique issues.
This year, the righthander had a 4.60 ERA overall and a 2.84 ERA in the two months before getting hurt.
The Red Sox’ top setup options for lefthanded closer Aroldis Chapman remain righthander Garrett Whitlock, lefthander Erik Miller, and righthander Tyron Guerrero. They expect Guerrero back from the IL as soon as Wednesday.
“[Slaten is] an important arm,” Tracy said, “but we have to deal with it and move on.”
Crochet builds up workload
Back at Fenway Park, Garrett Crochet on endured his heaviest workload yet in his bid to return for the playoffs, a 30-pitch bullpen session across two simulated innings.
“Everything went well,” Tracy said. “That was the most volume he’s had, so we’ll see over the next couple of days how he feels and go from there.”
Among other rehabbing pitchers: Tanner Houck made his third rehab appearance and first for Triple-A Worcester, striking out three of four batters (and walking the other). He threw 22 pitches but only 11 strikes.
The Sox’ plan calls for Houck to pitch for Worcester again late this week, throwing 50 or more pitches in a much longer relief appearance. For playoff purposes, they are keeping their options open, experimenting with Houck in short and long relief.
Progress for Mead
Seven weeks after fracturing his left wrist in his first game with the Red Sox, Curtis Mead is starting a hitting progression.
The infielder is due to begin “tee work” with an “underloaded,” lighter-than-normal bat on Wednesday, Tracy said. An ability to swing comfortably has held back Mead, who for weeks has been throwing/playing catch (including recently actually catching the ball thrown back to him).
Also in a race against the calendar, Mead appears unlikely to return this year unless the Red Sox play deep into the postseason
The running man
Ceddanne Rafaela (right quad strain) has “started to increase running volume” and will continue to do so the next several days, Tracy said. The center fielder has said he hopes to return this weekend when the Red Sox visit the Rays . . . Tracy and his staff gathered for a group dinner Monday, their first time doing so since Kansas City in mid-May. “So to be able to get all of us together and have a meal, it was a nice off day,” he said. Who paid? “The Red Sox.”

Over the last few weeks, the Boston Red Sox have gotten positive updates left and right about injured starting pitchers.
First and foremost, Garrett Crochet has been throwing and is trending towards a late-season return in Boston's bullpen, barring a setback. Tanner Houck has been on a minor league rehab assignment and is trending up. Plus, the current expectation is that Johan Oviedo is nearing a minor league rehab assignment as well. Now, it sounds like another hurler is trending up as well. On Tuesday, Tommy Cassell of the Worcester T&G Sports reported that there have been "some rumblings" that Kutter Crawford could join Triple-A Worcester throughout the week as well.
"And there are some rumblings that Kutter Crawford could be in Worcester this week, too," Cassell wrote. "The 30-year-old righty has been sidelined since March with right wrist and forearm issues and made one rehab stint with Worcester on April 11 before being shut down again. Crawford hasn’t been confirmed yet whether he will pitch in Worcester."
Kutter Crawford Is Trending Up
How about that?
Crawford hasn't been talked about in a long time. Now, it seems like the righty could potentially be in Worcester this week. Things move quickly in baseball, to say the least.
Crawford missed the entire 2025 season and he was trending up at one point early in the 2026 season and even went on a rehab assignment with Triple-A Worcester, although he suffered a setback and has been on the shelf ever since.
Now, of course, this doesn't guarantee that he will help the Red Sox before the 2026 season comes to a close. In fact, it arguably would be surprising to see him on the Red Sox's roster before the season comes to a close. Crawford's last appearance in a game was on April 11, 2026 with Worcester. When he does take the mound again, he's going to have to build up and get the rust off. The regular season will end for the Red Sox in just 12 days, as of writing, on Sep. 27. That's not a lot of time to begin a rehab assignment for the first time in five months and return to the majors with the playoffs looming.
But it's still good news in general for Boston. What if Crawford does pitch this week for Triple-A Worcester and looks like a game-changer? Maybe, he could surprise. Even if he doesn't, he's under team control for the 2027 and 2028 seasons. If the Red Sox could enter Spring Training with Crawford as a legit candidte for either the rotation — or even the bullpen — that makes the team better. Or, if he proves he's healthy, maybe he could even be an intriguing trade chip this winter.
All in all, hearing that one of the Red Sox's hurlers are trending up after missing so much time is positive in itself.

item.content:encoded:
A falta de dos semanas para que termine la temporada regular del 2026, todo parece indicar que los premios Cy Young de la Liga Americana y la Liga Nacional están prácticamente definidos.
Esto tiene poco que ver con el resto de los candidatos, que conforman un grupo sólido en ambas ligas, y mucho más con los líderes de la carrera. Cam Schlittler, de los Yankees, y Jacob Misiorowski, de los Cerveceros, simplemente les han cerrado la puerta a sus perseguidores. Ambos lanzadores de poder fueron elegidos de manera unánime en sus respectivas ligas por nuestro panel de 32 votantes de MLB.com y MLB Español en nuestra última encuesta del Cy Young del año.
Los expertos emitieron sus votos por quienes creen que se llevarán el galardón, tomando en cuenta no sólo los resultados hasta ahora, sino también cómo esperan que se desarrollen las últimas dos semanas. A los votantes se les pidió ordenar a sus cinco principales candidatos en cada liga, y los lanzadores recibieron puntos en una escala de 5-4-3-2-1: cinco puntos por un voto al primer lugar, cuatro por uno al segundo y así sucesivamente. Estos son los resultados.
A menos que se indique lo contrario, todas las estadísticas incluyen los juegos disputados hasta el domingo.
Schlittler blanqueó a los Mets durante seis innings en el último juego de la Serie del Subway el domingo, reduciendo su efectividad de la temporada a 1.95. No sólo es la mejor marca de la Liga Americana, sino que además está empatado con Misiorowski con la más baja entre los lanzadores calificados de Grandes Ligas. Schlittler ha permitido una carrera o menos en cada una de sus últimas siete aperturas, cerrando con broche de oro su primera temporada completa en las Mayores. Sigue dominando a los bateadores con una combinación de tres tipos de recta, la misma fórmula que utilizó para irrumpir en escena durante la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana en la postemporada pasada. Con octubre a la vuelta de la esquina, otra gran actuación en los playoffs podría estar muy cerca.
Cease ha estado sencillamente brillante en el primer año del contrato de siete temporadas que firmó con los Azulejos en noviembre pasado. Sumó nueve ponches en su apertura más reciente, el domingo ante los Orioles, su 13er juego de la temporada con nueve o más abanicados, más que cualquier otro lanzador de la Liga Americana. Los 236 ponches de Cease representan una nueva marca personal en una campaña y lo tienen empatado con Misiorowski con la mayor cantidad en Grandes Ligas. Este año, Cease ha utilizado un repertorio más equilibrado para complementar su letal combinación de recta de cuatro costuras y slider, dándole distintas maneras de enfrentar a las alineaciones rivales. Ésa es parte de la razón por la que el promedio de bateo de .177 en su contra es el más bajo entre los lanzadores calificados de la Liga Americana.
Quizás no esté al mismo nivel que Schlittler o Cease, pero Messick ha estado indiscutiblemente fantástico en su temporada de novato. El zurdo de peculiar mecánica permitió apenas una carrera en 5.1 innings en su apertura más reciente contra los Mellizos el viernes y, aun en plena lucha por los playoffs, eso es simplemente lo que hace Messick. Schlittler y Cease son los únicos dos lanzadores de la Liga Americana con más presentaciones de cinco o más entradas permitiendo una carrera o menos esta temporada. La efectividad de 2.51 de Messick es la quinta mejor de Grandes Ligas. La recta de cuatro costuras ha sido la clave de su éxito. Aunque Messick no lanza particularmente fuerte, con un promedio de apenas 94.3 mph, su recta de cuatro costuras ha sido uno de los pitcheos individuales más valiosos de Grandes Ligas, según la métrica de valor de carreras de Statcast.
El viernes, los Rays se convirtieron en el primer equipo en asegurar un boleto a la postemporada este año gracias a un dramático jonrón del dominicano Junior Caminero para dejar en el terreno al rival. Pero tampoco hay que olvidar a Rasmussen, quien abrió el juego por Tampa Bay y navegó sin mayores problemas durante siete entradas de una carrera. No debería sorprender que los Rays hayan ganado, porque eso es precisamente lo que hacen cuando Rasmussen sube a la lomita: han ganado cada una de sus últimas 10 aperturas, una racha que se remonta a la pausa del Juego de Estrellas. El derecho de 31 años se ubica entre los cinco mejores de la Liga Americana en efectividad (2.81), WHIP (0.92) y promedio de bateo en contra (.203), apoyándose en tres variantes de recta y un comando impecable.
Boston avanza con paso firme hacia un boleto a la postemporada respaldado por uno de los mejores cuerpos de lanzadores del béisbol. Esa frase habría tenido sentido en el Día Inaugural, pero no si se hubiera sabido que el zurdo Garrett Crochet estaría fuera de acción desde finales de abril. En ausencia de Crochet, Gray ha asumido el papel de as. Tiene marca de 17-5 con efectividad de 2.76 en 27 aperturas y, aunque las victorias de un lanzador no lo son todo, vale la pena destacar que ningún pitcher de la Liga Americana tiene más triunfos que Gray. Busca terminar por tercera vez en su carrera entre los cinco primeros en la votación del Premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana: fue segundo con los Mellizos en el 2023 y terminó tercero con los Atléticos en el 2015.
Otros que recibieron votos: Reid Detmers, Angelinos; Gavin Williams, Guardianes; Nick Martínez, Rays; Michael Wacha, Reales
LIGA NACIONAL
El Miz dejó atrás un inusual tropiezo con una sensacional apertura el martes pasado, dominando a los Cachorros durante 6.1 innings de una carrera y nueve ponches. El imponente derecho lidera a los lanzadores de la Liga Nacional en casi todas las categorías estadísticas, incluyendo efectividad (1.95), promedio de bateo en contra (.155) y ponches (236). Incluso con 161.1 entradas a cuestas, Misiorowski sigue lanzando fuego. Ya ha realizado 1,010 pitcheos a 100 mph o más esta temporada, más del doble que el lanzador que le sigue (Mason Miller, 468).
El eterno maravilla ha hecho todo lo posible por cerrar la brecha en la lucha por el Premio Cy Young de la Liga Nacional en la recta final. La efectividad de 2.18 de Sale es la segunda mejor de la Liga Nacional y la más baja para el lanzador de 37 años en una temporada desde el 2018. Ha sido notablemente consistente, permitiendo tres carreras o menos en cada una de sus últimas 23 aperturas. Ningún otro abridor ha tenido una racha de más de 16 juegos consecutivos permitiendo tres anotaciones o menos esta temporada. Sale está desafiando el paso del tiempo gracias, en parte, a una mejor velocidad, lanzando más fuerte que nunca como abridor.
Sánchez cayó un puesto con respecto a nuestra encuesta anterior después de permitir nueve carreras en sus últimas dos aperturas. Aun así, el espigado zurdo dominicano está armando una temporada que merece mucha consideración para el Cy Young. Sánchez ha lanzado la segunda mayor cantidad de innings en el béisbol (187.1), con la quinta mejor efectividad (2.79) y el tercer mejor FIP (2.72) entre los lanzadores calificados de la Liga Nacional. Según la versión de WAR de Baseball Reference, Sánchez ha sido el pitcher más valioso de la Gran Carpa en el 2026, acumulando 7.6 de WAR.
Luzardo se mete en nuestra encuesta final del Cy Young impulsado por una brillante blanqueada contra los Bravos, líderes del Este de la Liga Nacional, en el Día del Trabajo. Ya era hora de que el zurdo peruano-venezolano recibiera el reconocimiento que merece. Luzardo tiene marca de 8-1 con efectividad de 1.66 en sus últimas 12 aperturas, registrando la mejor efectividad de Grandes Ligas desde el 1ro de julio y ganando el premio al Lanzador del Mes de la Liga Nacional en agosto. Respaldado por un letal sweeper que desarrolló la temporada pasada, Luzardo posee la segunda tasa de ponches más alta (30.4%) de la Liga Nacional. Los aficionados de los Filis están a la expectativa después de que Luzardo se perdiera su última apertura debido a una molestia en el hombro, aunque dijo que “no estaba preocupado” tras someterse a una resonancia magnética.
Nos hemos acostumbrado a esperar tanto de Yamamoto que incluso sus mejores actuaciones parecen rutinarias, como su joya de siete entradas y 10 ponches contra los Rojos la noche del miércoles pasado. Sigue siendo el as de una rotación repleta de estrellas digna de Hollywood, con efectividad de 2.62 en 26 aperturas. Pocos lanzadores son mejores que Yamamoto a la hora de mantener corredores fuera de las bases, ya que su WHIP de 0.88 y su promedio de bateo en contra de .184 ocupan el segundo lugar en el Viejo Circuito, sólo por detrás de Misiorowski.
Otros que recibieron votos: Chase Burns, Rojos; el venezolano Eduardo Rodríguez, Diamondbacks; Mason Miller, Padres; Zack Wheeler, Filis

item.description: With two weeks to go in the 2026 regular season, it sure looks like the AL and NL Cy Young Awards are all but wrapped up. With two weeks to go in the 2026 regular season, it sure looks like the AL and NL Cy Young Awards are all but wrapped up.
This has little to do with the field -- which is strong in both leagues -- and more to do with the frontrunners. The Yankees' Cam Schlittler and the Brewers' Jacob Misiorowski have simply slammed the door shut. Both high-octane hurlers were a unanimous choice in their respective leagues among our panel of 32 MLB.com voters in our final Cy Young poll of the year.
The experts cast their votes for who they think will take home the hardware based not only on the results so far, but also how they expect the final two weeks to shake out. Voters were asked to rank their top five picks in each league, with pitchers receiving points on a 5-4-3-2-1 scale -- five points for a first-place vote, four points for a second-place vote and so on.
Unless otherwise noted, all stats are through play on Sunday.
AMERICAN LEAGUE
Schlittler blanked the Mets across six innings in the Subway Series finale on Sunday, lowering his season ERA to 1.95. Not only is that the best mark in the AL, it's also tied with Misiorowski for the lowest among qualified pitchers in the Majors. Schlittler has now allowed one run or fewer in each of his last seven starts, closing his first full Major League season with a flourish. He continues to overwhelm hitters with a three-fastball combo, the same formula that he used to burst onto the scene in the AL Wild Card Series last postseason. With October looming, an encore is right around the corner.
Cease has been nothing short of brilliant in the first year of a seven-year deal that he signed with the Blue Jays last November. He notched nine strikeouts in his most recent outing on Sunday against the Orioles, his 13th game this season with nine or more strikeouts -- more than any other AL pitcher. Cease's 236 strikeouts are a new single-season high and tied with Misiorowski for the most in the Majors. This year, Cease has used a more balanced pitch mix to supplement his lethal four-seam fastball/slider combo, giving him different ways to navigate opposing lineups. It's part of the reason why Cease's .177 batting average against is lowest among qualified AL pitchers.
He may not be on the same level as Schlittler or Cease, but Messick has been undeniably fantastic in his rookie season. The funky left-hander allowed just one run in 5 1/3 innings in his last start against the Twins on Friday and, even in the heat of the pennant race, that is simply what Messick does. Schlittler and Cease are the only two AL pitchers to have more outings of five or more innings while allowing one run or fewer this season. Messick's 2.51 ERA is fifth best in the Majors. The four-seam fastball is the key to his success. Though Messick doesn't throw hard -- sitting just 94.3 mph -- his four-seamer has been one of the most valuable individual pitches in the Majors, according to Statcast's run value metric.
On Friday, the Rays became the first team to clinch a postseason berth this year thanks to a dramatic walk-off home run from Junior Caminero. Not to be forgotten, Rasmussen started the game for Tampa Bay and breezed through seven innings of one-run ball. It shouldn't be a surprise that the Rays won because that is what they do when Rasmussen is on the hill: They have won each of his last 10 starts, a stretch that dates back to the All-Star break. The 31-year-old right-hander ranks in the top five in the AL in ERA (2.81), WHIP (0.92) and batting average against (.203), relying on three fastball shapes and impeccable command.
Boston is coasting toward a postseason berth behind one of baseball's best pitching staffs. That sentence would have made sense on Opening Day, but not if you knew that left-hander Garrett Crochet would be sidelined since late April. In Crochet's absence, Gray has stepped up as the ace. He is 17-5 with a 2.76 ERA in 27 starts, and while pitcher wins aren't everything, it's noteworthy that no AL pitcher has more wins than Gray. He is vying for his third career top-five finish in AL Cy Young Award voting: He was the runner up with the Twins in 2023 and finished No. 3 with the Athletics in 2015.
Others receiving votes: Reid Detmers, Angels; Gavin Williams, Guardians; Nick Martinez, Rays; Michael Wacha, Royals
NATIONAL LEAGUE
The Miz put a rare blip behind him with a sensational start last Tuesday, stifling the Cubs over 6 1/3 innings of one-run ball with nine strikeouts. The overpowering righty leads NL pitchers in nearly every statistical category, including ERA (1.95), batting average against (.155) and K's (236). Even with 161 1/3 innings under his belt, Misiorowski continues to bring the heat, too. He has now thrown 1,010 pitches at 100 mph or harder this season, more than double the next closest pitcher (Mason Miller, 468).
The ageless wonder has tried his best to close the gap in the NL Cy Young Award race down the stretch. Sale's 2.18 ERA is the second best in the NL and the lowest by the 37-year-old in a single season since 2018. He's been remarkably consistent, allowing three runs or fewer in each of his last 23 starts. No other starting pitcher has a stretch of more than 16 consecutive games allowing three runs or fewer this season. Sale is defying Father Time thanks in part to improved velocity, throwing harder than he ever has as a starting pitcher.
Sánchez dropped a spot from our previous poll after allowing nine runs across his last two starts. Still, the lanky left-hander is putting together a season that merits plenty of Cy Young consideration. Sánchez has pitched the second-most innings in baseball (187 1/3) with the fifth best ERA (2.79) and third best FIP (2.72) among qualified NL pitchers. By Baseball Reference's version of WAR, Sánchez has been the most valuable pitcher in baseball in 2026, tallying 7.6 WAR.
Luzardo cracks our final Cy Young poll on the backs of a brilliant shutout against the NL East-leading Braves on Labor Day. It's well past time that the left-hander receives his flowers. Luzardo is 8-1 with a 1.66 ERA in his last 12 starts, posting the lowest ERA in the Majors since July 1 and winning the NL Pitcher of the Month Award in August. Buoyed by a lethal sweeper that he developed last season, Luzardo has the second-highest strikeout rate (30.4%) in the National League. Phillies fans are holding their breath after Luzardo missed his last start due to a shoulder ailment, though he said he was "not concerned" following his MRI.
We have come to expect so much of Yamamoto that even his best performances feel routine -- like his seven-inning, 10-strikeout gem against the Reds last Wednesday. He is still the ace of a star-studded rotation befitting Hollywood, with a 2.62 ERA through 26 starts. Few pitchers are better at limiting traffic than Yamamoto, whose 0.88 WHIP and .184 batting average against are each second in the NL behind Misiorowski.
Others receiving votes: Chase Burns, Reds; Eduardo Rodriguez, D-backs; Mason Miller, Padres; Zack Wheeler, Phillies

item.content:encoded:
Now is not the time, of course, what with the Red Sox in a playoff push and all.
But deep down inside, in a maybe-one-day-eventually sort of way, Garrett Whitlock harbors aspirations to try again to be a starting pitcher, to return to the rotation.
Consider it a curiosity.
“I definitely know my body better and know everything better now, and so it’s definitely something I’d be open to. Will I?” Whitlock said. “I’m not going to walk into [chief baseball officer Craig Breslow’s] office and be like, ‘Hey, I’m starting.’ So it’s one of those things where the team would have to be on board with it and just talk through everything and go through it. But it’s something I’d always be open to.”
Whitlock is intrigued enough to have picked the brain in recent months of Griffin Jax, the righthander whom the Rays converted from reliever to starter this season.
Jax, 31, had an 8.00 ERA in 11 relief appearances, moved to the rotation in April, slowly built up his pitch count, and has a 3.59 ERA in 20 starts.
Whitlock and Jax became buddies when they played together for Team USA during the World Baseball Classic in March. They’ve texted about what amounts to an experiment for Jax.
Jax’s take, per Whitlock: Everything he learned in his years as a reliever, several as a high-end reliever, made him a better pitcher, regardless of role. Tweaks to his repertoire, knowing how to attack hitters, and ensuring his body recovers between outings — it all applies to being a starter.
Whitlock has had similar conversations with the Cubs’ Clay Holmes, another Team USA teammate. He made the switch last year.
“We all joke that we’re all failed starters,” Whitlock said of his bullpen brethren.
Take it from the Royals’ Seth Lugo, who beat the Red Sox on Friday.
He and Whitlock have had very similar career arcs: They reached the majors in their mid-20s as non-elite prospects, bounced between the bullpen and rotation based on team need and their performance, and accepted their club wanting them in a relief role. They were excellent at it.
All along, Lugo, a consummate pro and good employee in his years as a Mets reliever, said he wanted to give starting another go — someday. Now, he is in his fourth season and third contract since getting the chance — once he became a free agent — and turning it into a successful and lucrative second act.
“It’s not as daunting as it seems,” Lugo said at Fenway Park over the weekend. “What happens is you first get to the big leagues and you try to be someone that you’re not, just from other influences, other recommendations. But you [learn] how to get guys out [as a reliever].
“Once you make the switch back, you have the confidence. The problems you had earlier in your career, [which] sent you to the ’pen in the first place — you’re aware why those mistakes happened.”
Lugo, like Whitlock, was a late-innings arm. He faced the other team’s best hitters in some of the most important moments of the game.
“Once you have success pitching the seventh, eighth, ninth inning, the first six innings become a lot easier,” he said. “As a reliever, when you’re going into a game, you’re a lot more stressed out than you are as a starter. So you start to recognize what you’re good at, how you can get out of those situations.”
Whitlock, who possesses a 1.81 ERA in 51 relief appearances this year, last made more than a handful of starts in 2023. Since then, he ditched the four-seam fastball to lean even more on his sinker, went with a slider instead of a sweeper, and changed his changeup, which has become highly effective.
In discussing the possibility, Whitlock is a realist: The Sox’ rotation seems full for the foreseeable future.
His contract includes team options for 2027 ($8.25 million) and 2028 ($10.5 million). Those are good deals for an elite reliever — and a really good deal for even a serviceable starter.
“I doubt Boston will do it. We’re pretty good on starting depth,” Whitlock said. “If I become a free agent and a team approaches me about it, I’m open to it and see how it goes.”
Perez on Abreu
Royals icon and Venezuela captain Salvador Perez, witness to Wilyer Abreu’s WBC star turn, is a big fan — and a big believer of Abreu on a big stage. “He’s going to be the MVP if Boston makes it to the World Series,” Perez said. “He’s built for a moment like that.” … Early returns on Adley Rutschman’s cortisone shot last week, intended to alleviate pain in his right elbow, are solid. Against Kansas City, he went 3 for 10 with a double, as many walks as strikeouts (two) — and played three games in a row for the first time since getting hurt. “It definitely helped a lot,” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “You can tell his body language and stuff too, he looks and feels pretty good.” … Garrett Crochet’s bullpen session Tuesday is scheduled for 30 pitches across two simulated innings, a step up from previous shorter sessions.

We've reached the "wake me up for the playoffs" portion of the Boston Red Sox season.
The Red Sox have 12 games remaining on their 2026 regular-season schedule. As of Monday, they sit comfortably in the second American League Wild Card spot with a six-game lead. They're 4.5 games behind the New York Yankees in the Wild Card standings, so barring a shocking development, they'll visit the New York Yankees in the Wild Card Series for the second consecutive year.
Which 26 players will the Red Sox bring with them to the Bronx? Who's on the chopping block? Here's our 26-man playoff roster projection with 15 days until Game 1:
MORE RED SOX
Catcher (2): Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
Cuts: None
The Red Sox could theoretically cut Wong since he'd barely see the field with Rutschman healthy. If Rutschman went down in that scenario, Mickey Gasper could go behind the plate... but that wouldn't be pretty.
Here's the problem with that approach: If Rutschman gets hurt and the Red Sox add a replacement catcher mid-series, Rutschman would be ineligible for the next playoff round. So if he got hurt in the Wild Card Series, he'd be ineligible for the ALDS and eligible to return in the ALCS.
Putting Wong on the playoff roster ensures that if Rutschman goes down, they won't need to add a mid-series replacement with Wong and Gasper already on board. And while Wong isn't exactly Pudge Rodriguez defensively, he's better than Gasper behind the dish.
Infield (7): Willson Contreras, Trevor Story, Caleb Durbin, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Nick Sogard, Mickey Gasper, Andruw Monasterio
Cuts: Curtis Mead (IL), Anthony Seigler (IL)
Even with Wong on the roster, Gasper's incredible offensive upside shown in August earns him a roster spot as a bench bat. Monasterio is on the bubble, but recent injuries may have cleared his path to a bench role.
It doesn't look like Mead (wrist) will be healthy in time for the start of the postseason.
Outfield (5): Jarren Duran, Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
Cuts: Eli White (IL), Masataka Yoshida (IL), Nate Eaton
The big question mark here is White's health, as the speedster was recently placed on the 10-day injured list with a foot ligament injury. He'll play a key bench role if healthy, but if he isn't, Jones or Eaton are the top candidates for that fifth outfield spot. We're leaning Jones because of his ability to mash left-handers.
Yoshida (hamstring) probably isn't coming back this year.
Starting rotation (3): Sonny Gray, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suarez
Cuts: Patrick Sandoval
Sandoval just hasn't been reliable, so he draws the short straw. Jake Bennett and the returning Garrett Crochet move to the bullpen -- assuming Crochet is healthy enough to give one or two quality innings in relief.
Bullpen (9): Garrett Crochet, Jake Bennett, Brayan Bello, Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, Erik Miller, Tyron Guerrero, Garrett Whitlock, Aroldis Chapman
Cuts: Justin Slaten (IL), Tanner Houck (IL), Johan Oviedo (IL), Alec Gamboa, Jovani Moran, Raymond Burgos
If Slaten's elbow is healthy, he's in, but it doesn't currently look like it will be since he was recently shut down from throwing.
Crochet is trending toward being ready just in time for October. So is Houck, but he hasn't pitched in a big-league game since May 2025, and he hasn't looked sharp in his rehab outings. While his upside is intriguing, we'd leave him off the initial playoff roster.
Brayan Bello makes the cut as a bulk arm after excelling in that role throughout the second half.

The American League East has always been the sport's most star-driven division, even when the standings don't always show it. The New York Yankees-Boston Red Sox rivalry alone has produced decades of this, but it's not just those two anymore.
The Toronto Blue Jays have peaked into a real contender, the Tampa Bay Rays are leading this year's race and continue to develop, and the Baltimore Orioles are always one prospect wave away from popping off again. With that much noise in one division, it's easy to lose track of just how much individual talent is walking around it.
Case in point: with Tarik Skubal now pitching for the Los Angeles Dodgers, this year's AL Cy Young race is shaping up to be a battle between two AL East arms, Cam Schlittler and Dylan Cease. That trophy is staying in this division no matter what. But for Red Sox fans, it's worth saying the obvious: if Garrett Crochet had stayed healthy all year, he'd be right in that conversation too, not watching it from the outside looking in.
A healthy Garrett Crochet would've made the 2026 AL Cy Young Award race more interesting
It's easy to forget just how dominant Crochet was in 2025. He went 18-5 with a 2.59 ERA across a league-leading 205.1 innings, struck out a league-best 255 batters, and finished as the AL Cy Young runner-up behind Skubal himself. Take a quick glance at his Baseball Savant page from that season and it reads like a cheat code, elite percentile marks across nearly every meaningful category a pitcher can be graded on. That's the version of Crochet the division rivals were supposed to get again in 2026.
Instead, he was clearly not right from the start, posting an ugly-looking 6.30 ERA across his first six starts before landing on the injured list on April 29 with a shoulder issue that turned into a lat problem after a setback in May. The strikeouts were still there (37 in just 30 innings), but the results were far from pretty, and Boston has been without its ace for basically the entire season since.
Here's where it gets exciting again, though. Crochet threw a bullpen session at Fenway this week, his second since resuming throwing, and interim manager Chad Tracy has been candid that a return this season likely means relief work, not a return to the rotation. Crochet has relief experience already from earlier in his career, and has shown flashes of pure domincance. In 72 bullpen appearances, he logged 73 innings with 85 punchies and 2.71 ERA. In his four postseason relief outings, he has a 0.00 ERA and has struck out 6 of the 14 batters he faced.
He's also made it clear he has zero ego about the role. With Boston fighting to hold onto that second Wild Card spot, a healthy Crochet coming out of the bullpen in high-leverage October moments would be about as fun a development as this fanbase could ask for down the stretch.
